3-arts-club-cafe.text: The Gold Coast landmark was built in 1915 for the Three Arts Club, founded in 1912 — a Holabird & Roche building with 92 residence rooms where young women studying music, drama and painting could live safely. More than 13,000 women stayed there before the last residents moved out in 2004. It was designated a Chicago Landmark in 1981, and Restoration Hardware now owns the space, running the Three Arts Cafe inside.
3-arts-club-cafe.descriptor: Café inside the 1914 Three Arts Club building, now RH Chicago on N Dearborn

360-chicago.text: The observatory floor sits 1,030 feet above the street in the tower long known as the John Hancock Center. Independently run and rebranded 360 Chicago in 2014, it added TILT that same summer — floor-to-ceiling windows that slowly tilt visitors out to 30 degrees over the street — alongside an open-air SkyWalk and the CloudBar cocktail lounge.
360-chicago.descriptor: 94th-floor observation deck in the former John Hancock Center

5-rabanitos.text: Chef Alfonso Sotelo's Pilsen restaurant opened this Hyde Park second location in early 2025, in a University of Chicago-owned 53rd Street storefront that had sat empty since The Budlong Hot Kitchen closed in 2023. The name comes from Sotelo's childhood in Guerrero, where he and his four siblings sold radishes off the family farm and got called "cinco rabanitos."
5-rabanitos.descriptor: Regional Mexican from Pilsen's 5 Rabanitos, on E. 53rd St in Hyde Park

5-rabanitos-restaurante-and-taqueria.text: Alfonso Sotelo opened 5 Rabanitos at 18th and Wood in 2015, a block from the National Museum of Mexican Art. He came to California from Guerrero at 15, worked his way up to head chef at the now-closed West Town Tavern, then went out on his own; the name recalls his childhood, when he and his four siblings sold radishes from the family farm and were known as "cinco rabanitos."
5-rabanitos-restaurante-and-taqueria.descriptor: Regional Mexican taqueria at 18th & Wood in Pilsen, open since 2015

aba.text: Aba is chef CJ Jacobson's Mediterranean restaurant for Lettuce Entertain You, three floors up in Fulton Market with a plant-filled rooftop that has made it an extremely popular summertime destination. The kitchen runs four hummus variations — classic, smoky garlic, wild mushroom and short rib — alongside shawarma-spiced skirt steak and whipped feta.
aba.descriptor: Rooftop Mediterranean restaurant on the 3rd floor at 302 N. Green St.

abraham-lincoln-the-head-of-state.text: Augustus Saint-Gaudens designed this brooding seated Lincoln to evoke the loneliness and burden of command; a 1904 studio fire destroyed his drawings and models and he died in 1907, so the work was only completed in 1908. It was displayed at the Metropolitan Museum and at the 1915 San Francisco world's fair before it was finally unveiled in Grant Park on May 31, 1926, on a 150-foot exedra designed by Stanford White.
abraham-lincoln-the-head-of-state.descriptor: Saint-Gaudens' seated Lincoln bronze in Grant Park, on a Stanford White exedra

writtenFor.name: Abraham Lincoln: The Head of State

abraham-lincoln-the-man.text: Augustus Saint-Gaudens's 12-foot bronze, finished in 1887 and known everywhere as the Standing Lincoln, shows Lincoln rising from a chair of state to speak; Stanford White designed the pedestal and exedra around it in Lincoln Park. Chicago businessman Eli Bates left $40,000 for the statue, and Saint-Gaudens worked from a life mask and hand casts taken of Lincoln in 1860. Recasts stand in London and Mexico City.
abraham-lincoln-the-man.descriptor: Saint-Gaudens's 1887 'Standing Lincoln' bronze in Lincoln Park

akahoshi-ramen.text: Mike Satinover left a marketing research career and toured pop-ups as Reddit's 'Ramen Lord' before opening Akahoshi in Logan Square with no formal restaurant training. The name means 'red star' — a symbol shared by Sapporo and Chicago — and he works the bowls like a lab, using a refractometer on the broth and controlling noodle hydration. Bon Appétit named it one of the 20 best new restaurants of 2024.
akahoshi-ramen.descriptor: Logan Square ramen shop from Reddit's 'Ramen Lord' on N California Ave

al-capones-house.text: Al Capone moved into this Park Manor two-flat at 7244 S. Prairie Ave. on August 8, 1923 — a six-bedroom, two-story building put up in 1905 on a 68-foot-wide double lot, bought for $5,500. It was his Chicago home in the years he built up the city's Prohibition rackets, and it is an ordinary South Side brick house rather than a gangster's mansion.
al-capones-house.descriptor: Al Capone's 1920s family two-flat on S Prairie Ave in Park Manor

albert-ivar-goodman-theatre.text: The Goodman was founded in 1925 as a memorial to playwright Kenneth Sawyer Goodman, who died in the 1918 flu pandemic, and won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 1992. It moved in 2000 to 170 N. Dearborn, where its two auditoriums — the Albert and the Owen — sit inside the landmarked 1922 Harris and Selwyn theaters, gutted and rebuilt behind their preserved facades.
albert-ivar-goodman-theatre.descriptor: Goodman Theatre mainstage at 170 N Dearborn in the Loop theater district

alfred-caldwell-lily-pool.text: Landscape architect Alfred Caldwell rebuilt an 1889 Victorian lily pond into this hidden Prairie School garden between 1936 and 1938. Zoo director Marlin Perkins turned it into a bird sanctuary called the Rookery in the 1950s, and grazing and neglect left what Caldwell later called "a dead world." A $1.2 million restoration finished in 2002, and the 2.7-acre pool became a National Historic Landmark in 2006.
alfred-caldwell-lily-pool.descriptor: Hidden Prairie-style garden pool in Lincoln Park, a National Historic Landmark

alhambra-palace.text: A 24,000-square-foot hall on West Loop's Restaurant Row seating roughly 1,400, done up in ornate tilework, gold leaf and plush fabrics. Belly dancers, live acoustic music and DJ nights run alongside the tagines, kebabs and mezze, and its eight themed rooms and multi-level layout handle private parties from 50 up to 1,200 guests.
alhambra-palace.descriptor: Middle Eastern palace with belly dancers on Randolph's Restaurant Row

alinea.text: Opened in 2005 by chef Grant Achatz and Nick Kokonas, Alinea built its name on theatrical, maximalist modernist cooking. It won the James Beard award for Outstanding Restaurant in 2016 and held three Michelin stars from 2011 until it was cut to two in November 2025.
alinea.descriptor: Grant Achatz's modernist tasting-menu restaurant on N Halsted, Lincoln Park

als-beef.text: Al's has been making Italian beef since 1938, when Al Ferreri started it with his sister Frances and brother-in-law Chris Pacelli Sr.; a grandson of the founder still runs the company, which operates a Taylor Street shop in Little Italy. The sandwich is the Chicago template: heavily seasoned roast beef in gravy on soft French bread with sweet or hot peppers.
als-beef.descriptor: Italian beef stand on Taylor Street in Little Italy

als-beef-lake-view-east.text: Al Ferreri, his sister Frances and brother-in-law Chris Pacelli Sr. opened the first Al's as a Taylor Street beef stand in Little Italy in 1938; the company still bills itself as "the beefstand that launched the national sandwich of Chicago." The order is heavily seasoned roast beef in gravy on French bread with sweet or hot peppers.
als-beef-lake-view-east.descriptor: Italian beef counter at 2804 N. Western Ave.; chain born on Taylor St. in 1938

als-beef-little-italy.text: Al's started as a beef stand on Taylor Street in Little Italy in 1938 under Albert Ferreri, and still bills itself as "the beefstand that launched the national sandwich of Chicago." The order to know: heavily seasoned roast beef on soft French bread, dipped in its own gravy, with sweet or hot peppers.
als-beef-little-italy.descriptor: Italian beef counter in Lakeview — Chicago chain founded on Taylor St in 1938

als-beef-river-north.text: Al's has been making Italian beef since 1938, when Al Ferreri started it with his sister Frances and brother-in-law Chris Pacelli Sr.; the Taylor Street shop in Little Italy is the chain's original location, and a grandson of the founder still runs the company. The sandwich is the Chicago template: heavily seasoned roast beef in gravy on soft French bread with sweet peppers or hot giardiniera.
als-beef-river-north.descriptor: Original 1938 Italian beef stand on Taylor Street in Little Italy

american-writers-museum.text: Opened in May 2017 on the second floor of 180 N. Michigan Avenue, it calls itself the only museum devoted to American writers and their works — founder Malcolm O'Hagan took the idea from the Dublin Writers Museum. Inside are a 60-foot timeline of 100 authors, a 'Surprise Bookshelf,' vintage typewriters visitors can type on, and the 'Word Waterfall' light installation.
american-writers-museum.descriptor: Museum devoted to American writers, 2nd floor of 180 N Michigan Ave

andies.text: Chef-owner Andie Tamras has run this Clark Street Mediterranean fusion room since 1974, building a menu of homemade pastas, sauces and seasonal dips from dishes he picked up traveling around the Mediterranean.
andies.descriptor: Mediterranean fusion mainstay on N. Clark St in Andersonville since 1974

ann-sather-restaurant.text: Ann Sather, the Swedish immigrant who ran this Lakeview diner, was retiring and closing up in 1981 when a young Tom Tunney talked her into selling it to him instead. He grew it into a small local chain and later spent two decades as 44th Ward alderman. The oversized cinnamon rolls that come with almost every order are what people actually come for.
ann-sather-restaurant.descriptor: Swedish-American diner on W Belmont known for giant cinnamon rolls

antique-taco.text: Rick and Ashley Ortiz built Antique Taco around the two things they collect — tacos and antiques — so the vintage pieces filling the Wicker Park dining room are part of the concept, some of them for sale. Regulars go for the crispy battered fish taco with smoky cabbage, the meatball slider under mole poblano, and rosemary margaritas poured from glass jugs.
antique-taco.descriptor: Taqueria on Milwaukee Ave. in Wicker Park, hung with antiques for sale

antique-taco-bridgeport.text: Antique Taco is a family business from Rick and Ashley Ortiz, who built it around what they describe as two things they loved: tacos and antiques — hence the vintage-furnished dining rooms. The Bridgeport shop on 35th Street is one of the couple's two Chicago locations, alongside the Wicker Park store on Milwaukee Avenue.
antique-taco-bridgeport.descriptor: Taco shop with vintage decor at 35th & Morgan in Bridgeport

apollo-theater.text: The Apollo is the off-Loop commercial house at 2550 N Lincoln Ave where "Million Dollar Quartet" moved in on October 31, 2008 and stayed until January 17, 2016 — a run of more than seven years, the third-longest-running show by calendar span in Chicago theater history. It still books open-ended commercial productions and touring shows.
apollo-theater.descriptor: Off-Loop commercial theater at 2550 N Lincoln Ave in Lincoln Park

arie-crown-theater.text: The theater is named for Arie Crown, the Lithuanian immigrant father of industrialist Henry Crown, and opened in 1960 with 5,000 seats — one of the largest houses in Chicago. A 1967 fire shut it until 1971, and later acoustic work reshaped the hall down to 4,188 seats. Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, the Rolling Stones, David Bowie and Aretha Franklin have all played it.

art-of-pizza.text: The Art of Pizza has served the Lakeview area for more than 30 years and sells its deep dish both by the whole pie and by the slice, in thin-crust and pan-stuffed styles. The restaurant cites a Chicago Tribune ranking that put its deep dish first, with judges praising a "near-perfect, golden-brown crust" and a sauce with "nice, herby flavors."
art-of-pizza.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish and stuffed pizza sold by the slice

aster-hall.text: Aster Hall opened for the 2018 holiday shopping season across the ground, fifth and sixth floors of the 900 North Michigan Shops — a 25,000-square-foot food hall of sixteen food and beverage vendors built by Brendan Sodikoff's Hogsalt group. Small Cheval anchors the food floor, and the sixth is a bar and lounge looking out over Michigan Avenue and the lake.
aster-hall.descriptor: Upscale food hall on the upper floors of the 900 N Michigan shops

athena-greek-restaurant.text: Athena's draw is its massive outdoor patio on Halsted Street with a close-up view of the city skyline, which makes it a warm-weather favorite. The kitchen sticks to Greektown standards — gyros, charbroiled octopus, lamb and artichokes in lemon sauce, fish roe spread, and honey-phyllo custard pastry for dessert.
athena-greek-restaurant.descriptor: Greek restaurant at 212 S. Halsted St. with a large patio in Greektown

athenian-room.descriptor: Greek room on W Webster in Lincoln Park since 1972; chicken over fries

au-cheval.text: Hogsalt's Au Cheval opened in 2012 at 800 W. Randolph in the West Loop, a compact all-day diner with counter and booth seating. Its cheeseburger — American cheese, dijonnaise, pickles, grilled onions — is called by many the best in Chicago, and the room is notoriously hard to get into: once the text says your table is ready, you have ten minutes to claim it.
au-cheval.descriptor: West Loop diner on W Randolph known for its cheeseburger, since 2012

auditorium-theatre.text: Adler and Sullivan's 1889 masterpiece was dedicated by President Benjamin Harrison on December 9, 1889, with opera star Adelina Patti singing that night. It was among the first buildings lit entirely by incandescent bulbs and carried one of the earliest central air-conditioning systems, and it was the first home of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. Roosevelt University has occupied the building since 1946.
auditorium-theatre.descriptor: 1889 Adler & Sullivan theater on Michigan Ave, inside Roosevelt University

avec.text: One Off Hospitality's second restaurant started life as a wine bar and made its name as much on the room as the food — it won a James Beard Award for Outstanding Restaurant Design in 2005. Chef and co-founder Paul Kahan took Beard's Best Chef: Great Lakes in 2004 and Outstanding Chef in 2013.
avec.descriptor: Mediterranean small plates and wine bar on West Randolph's restaurant row

bacci-pizzeria-portage-park.text: Bacci built its name on the Jumbo Slice — an oversized slice it bills as Chicago's original, first sold in 1996 at a shop on Taylor Street in Little Italy. It has since grown into multiple family-owned storefronts across Chicago and the suburbs, including this Milwaukee Avenue counter in Portage Park.
bacci-pizzeria-portage-park.descriptor: Jumbo-slice pizza counter on N. Milwaukee Ave in Portage Park

batcolumn.text: Claes Oldenburg's "Batcolumn" (1977) is a 101-foot baseball bat of gray latticework steel standing on its knob outside the Harold Washington Social Security building at 600 W. Madison. Oldenburg picked the bat as a stand-in for Chicago's ambition and vigor; it was meant to be red but was painted gray to keep it distinct from Calder's nearby "Flamingo." It drew protests at its dedication and is now a local favorite.
batcolumn.descriptor: 101-foot Claes Oldenburg baseball-bat sculpture on W. Madison St

batter-berries.text: Craig and Tanya Richardson opened Batter & Berries on North Lincoln Avenue in 2012, and the Black-owned brunch room made its name on the French toast flight — a sampler of thin, eggy slices in rotating flavors served with housemade maple butter. The other signature is the Cluk-N-Gaufre: pulled chicken in a sweet-potato waffle with a fried chicken breast on top.
batter-berries.descriptor: Lincoln Park brunch spot on N Lincoln Ave known for its French toast flight

bavettes-bar-boeuf.text: Bavette's is Hogsalt's steakhouse at 218 W. Kinzie in River North, done up in jazz-era decor with music to match. Steak frites is the headline, but Time Out's line is that the fried and roasted chicken rival the beef, and the pies — lemon meringue, chocolate cream — have their own following. Reservations open 21 days ahead at 9am; walk-ins may have better odds.
bavettes-bar-boeuf.descriptor: Jazz-era steakhouse at 218 W Kinzie in River North

beatnik.text: Beatnik opened in 2017 in the former Mecca Fashion building on Chicago Avenue, and the room is the point: Bonhomme's in-house design studio spent two years gathering antiques from around the world and filled the 6,000-square-foot, 200-seat space with them plus more than 400 living plants. The kitchen runs from the Eastern Mediterranean across North Africa and finishes in Mexico; the bar leans tropical.
beatnik.descriptor: Boho cocktail bar and Mediterranean restaurant on Chicago Ave in West Town

beatnik-on-the-river.text: Beatnik on the River, part of Bonhomme's Beatnik family alongside the West Town and Lincoln Park rooms, runs a menu that travels from the Eastern Mediterranean across Northern Africa and finishes with the flavors of Mexico, served inside bohemian interiors drawn from Morocco, the rustic Mediterranean countryside and Italy.
beatnik-on-the-river.descriptor: Globe-spanning small plates and cocktails at 180 N. Upper Wacker on the river

beatrix.text: Beatrix opened at Clark and Grand in June 2013 as a Lettuce Entertain You hybrid — coffeehouse, bakery and restaurant in one — and its menu was largely assembled from test-kitchen dishes that never found a home at the group's other restaurants. The honey butter cinnamon roll and the kale-based Emerald City salad are the ones people come back for.
beatrix.descriptor: All-day cafe, bakery and restaurant at Clark & Grand in River North

beatrix-streeterville.text: Beatrix is Lettuce Entertain You's all-day "healthy meets delicious" concept — from Rich Melman and Marc Jacobs with chef partners John Chiakulas, Rita Dever and Susan Weaver — that works as coffeehouse, bakery and restaurant at once, with Beatrix Coffee Roasters at the coffee bar. The house-baked cookies are what people walk out with.
beatrix-streeterville.descriptor: Lettuce Entertain You all-day cafe and bakery on N. St. Clair

beggars-pizza.text: Beggars began in 1976 as a single pizzeria in Blue Island, opened by Angelo Garetto, and spread across Illinois and northwest Indiana over nearly five decades on the strength of its thin crust and deep dish. It's a Chicago White Sox pizza partner and runs the Beggars Pizza Pub at the ballpark.
beggars-pizza.descriptor: West Loop branch of the South Side pizza chain, thin crust and deep dish

begin-route-66.text: This is the eastern end of Route 66: the "Begin Historic Illinois U.S. Route 66" markers stand on Adams Street at Michigan Avenue, where westbound drivers start the drive. The 1926 route actually began a block south at Jackson Boulevard; when Jackson became one-way eastbound in 1955 the westbound traffic was shifted north to Adams, which is why the "End" signs are still on Jackson.
begin-route-66.descriptor: "Begin Historic Route 66" sign on Adams St at Michigan Ave

belmont-harbor.text: Belmont Harbor provides about 730 moorings along with a fuel dock and a ship store, and the Chicago Yacht Club keeps a Belmont station here. Just inland is the Bill Jarvis Migratory Bird Sanctuary, first landscaped in the 1920s and nearly bulldozed for a golf course in 1968 until Lake View neighbors — including Bill Jarvis — led a successful campaign to save it; it now hosts more than 150 bird species.
belmont-harbor.descriptor: Lakefront marina with 730 moorings, in Lincoln Park off Addison St

berlin-wall-monument.text: A real section of the Berlin Wall stands inside the CTA's Western Brown Line station. The German government offered Chicago the piece in 2008, dedicated to the city's residents for helping "secure the freedom" of Berlin, and the city installed it in Lincoln Square — historically its most German-American neighborhood.
berlin-wall-monument.descriptor: Berlin Wall slab inside the Western Brown Line station, Lincoln Square

bessie-coleman.text: Bessie Coleman moved to Chicago in 1915 and worked as a manicurist; shut out of American flight schools, she was urged by Chicago Defender publisher Robert S. Abbott to train abroad and on June 15, 1921 became the first Black woman to earn an international pilot's license. 'Queen Bess' died in a 1926 crash, and 10,000 mourners attended her Chicago funeral. Her marker is one of the walk-of-fame plaques set along King Drive.
bessie-coleman.descriptor: Bronzeville Walk of Fame plaque on King Drive honoring the pioneer aviator

big-chicks.text: Michelle Fire opened Big Chicks on December 11, 1986 in what had been a veterans' bar, inheriting the old regulars and the bartenders along with the room. It has since become an informal gay community center for Uptown, hung with her own art collection, and was inducted into the Chicago LGBT Hall of Fame in 2016.
big-chicks.descriptor: Uptown gay bar open since 1986, hung with the owner's art collection

big-jones.text: Paul Fehribach and Mark Armantrout opened Big Jones in 2008 to cook regional Southern food out of the archives — antebellum heirloom grits, house charcuterie, revived historic dishes — sourced from local farms and Southern artisan producers. Fehribach is an eight-time James Beard Award semifinalist for Best Chef: Great Lakes and has written two books on the history of Southern cooking.
big-jones.descriptor: Heirloom Southern cooking on N Clark St in Andersonville since 2008

big-star.text: Big Star is a honky-tonk taqueria modeled on the bars of Bakersfield, California, with executive chef-partner Paul Kahan behind the food: house-made tortillas, tacos al pastor, Baja and panza, a soundtrack running classic country to '70s rock, and 20 exclusive house-barrel bourbons out of Kentucky. It spun off its own label, Big Star Recording Co., in 2016.
big-star.descriptor: Honky-tonk taqueria and bourbon bar at 1531 N Damen in Wicker Park

big-star-west-town.text: Big Star is the taco-and-whiskey bar from One Off Hospitality, the group behind The Publican, avec and The Violet Hour, whose partners Paul Kahan and Donnie Madia both hold James Beard awards. It serves a short menu of tacos, whiskey and beer in a lively, no-frills room, and has two Chicago locations: Wicker Park and Wrigleyville.
big-star-west-town.descriptor: Taco, whiskey and beer bar from One Off Hospitality

billy-goat-tavern.text: William "Billy Goat" Sianis opened his first tavern in 1934 and moved the business below street level at 430 N. Michigan in 1964, near the Tribune and Sun-Times offices. He is the source of the Curse of the Billy Goat: ejected with his pet goat from Game 4 of the 1945 World Series at Wrigley, he cursed the Cubs — who won no title until 2016.
billy-goat-tavern.descriptor: Below-street burger tavern on Lower Michigan Ave since 1964

billy-goat-tavern-grill.text: Greek immigrant William "Billy Goat" Sianis founded the Billy Goat in 1934; his ejection from Game 4 of the 1945 World Series along with his pet goat produced the Curse of the Billy Goat, which the Cubs didn't shake until 2016. The tavern is popularly tied to the Saturday Night Live "cheezborger, cheezborger — no Pepsi, Coke" sketch, though Dan Aykroyd said it actually drew on John Belushi's father's café. This is the Navy Pier outpost at 700 E. Grand.
billy-goat-tavern-grill.descriptor: Navy Pier outpost of the 1934 "cheezborger" tavern

billy-goat-tavern-west-loop.text: This is the Midway Airport outpost of Billy Goat Tavern, the griddle William "Billy Goat" Sianis opened in 1934 after buying a tavern with a check that bounced. In 1945 he was turned away from a World Series game at Wrigley with his pet goat and reportedly cursed the team — "them Cubs, they ain't gonna win no more" — a hex the Cubs didn't shake until 2016. It also inspired SNL's "cheezborger" sketch, though the attribution is disputed.
billy-goat-tavern-west-loop.descriptor: Billy Goat "cheezborger" counter at Midway Airport, Concourse A

billy-sunday.text: Chef Matthias Merges, a Charlie Trotter's alum, is behind Billy Sunday, whose back bar holds one of North America's largest collections of vintage fernet and amaro alongside a robust selection of rare scotch, bourbon and rum. Barkeep Alex Bachman's cocktails lean on unusual ingredients — a syrup made from maidenhair ferns, say — and there's an elevated bar menu to match.
billy-sunday.descriptor: Craft cocktail bar on Logan Boulevard with a huge amaro and fernet library

biograph-theatre.text: On July 22, 1934, John Dillinger walked out of the Biograph after a movie and was shot dead on the sidewalk by FBI agents led by Melvin Purvis. Designed by Samuel N. Crowen in 1914 in red pressed brick and white-glazed terra cotta, it is on the National Register (1984) and was made a Chicago Landmark in 2001; Victory Gardens Theater bought it in 2004 and reopened it as a live stage in 2006.
biograph-theatre.descriptor: 1914 movie house on Lincoln Ave, now Victory Gardens Theater

birrieria-zaragoza.text: Birrieria Zaragoza built its reputation on one dish: slow-cooked goat that never touches the consommé until it is plated, when some of the tomato-based broth is spooned over it. The family-owned original stands at 4852 S Pulaski Rd in Archer Heights; a second location opened in Uptown at 4800 N Broadway in 2023.
birrieria-zaragoza.descriptor: Family-run goat birria specialist on S Pulaski Rd in Archer Heights

bloomingdale-trail-park.text: The 606 runs on the Bloomingdale Line, a freight track built in 1873 by the Chicago & Pacific Railroad; the city bought the right-of-way from Canadian Pacific in January 2013 and opened the park on June 6, 2015. At 2.7 miles it's the longest elevated rail-to-trail greenway in the Western Hemisphere — and the name is an homage to 606, the prefix of nearly every Chicago ZIP code.
bloomingdale-trail-park.descriptor: The 606: 2.7-mile elevated rail-trail park above Bloomingdale Ave

blue-chicago.text: The building opened in the early 1970s as a dive country bar on a former used-car lot, drawing cops and neighborhood regulars, and reopened as Bluelight in September 2006 under the owners of Rebel Bar & Grill and Pitchfork. The blue neon marquee still advertises the draw — "the light is on til 4am" — and the house pour is the Bluelight Special: vodka, blue curaçao and pineapple in a 32-ounce mug.
blue-chicago.descriptor: Late-night dive bar on N Western Ave in Roscoe Village with a 4 a.m. license

blues-heaven-garden.text: The garden sits beside 2120 S. Michigan Ave., the Chess Records studio where Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley recorded from 1957 to 1967, and where the Rolling Stones cut an instrumental named for the address in 1964. Willie Dixon's widow Marie bought the building — a Chicago Landmark since 1990 — in 1993 and opened it as Blues Heaven in 1997; the foundation has run free Record Row concerts in the garden for more than two decades.
blues-heaven-garden.descriptor: Outdoor concert garden beside the old Chess Records studio on S. Michigan

boka.text: Boka opened in 2003 and became the seed of the Boka Restaurant Group, now one of Chicago's biggest restaurant families. Chef partner Lee Wolen took over the kitchen in 2014; the restaurant held a Michelin star every year from 2011 through 2025, and Wolen has collected multiple James Beard nominations and the Chicago Tribune's 2015 Chef of the Year.
boka.descriptor: Seasonal American fine dining from Boka Restaurant Group, open since 2003

bonci-pizza.text: Rome's Gabriele Bonci — the pizzaiolo behind Pizzarium, with some 1,500 pizza recipes to his name — makes rectangular Roman pizza al taglio from dough fermented 48 to 72 hours and sold by weight, with 12 to 15 varieties on display each day. The Diversey Parkway shop in Lincoln Park is one of four Chicago locations.
bonci-pizza.descriptor: Roman pizza al taglio sold by weight, W Diversey Pkwy in Lincoln Park

bonci-pizzeria.text: This West Loop counter at 161 N. Sangamon is the Chicago flagship of Roman pizzaiolo Gabriele Bonci, of Rome's Pizzarium. The pizza al taglio comes in long rectangles of 48–72-hour organic stone-ground dough, with 12 to 15 varieties displayed daily, weighed and priced by the piece — alongside supplì.
bonci-pizzeria.descriptor: Roman pizza al taglio by weight from Gabriele Bonci, 161 N Sangamon

brasa-roja-irving-park.descriptor: Colombian rotisserie chicken and char-broiled steak on N. Pulaski Rd

breakfast-house-west-town.text: This is the original Breakfast House: chef-owner Jaime opened it in West Town in 2012, and the family-run brunch spot has since grown to about ten locations around Chicago and one in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. The kitchen's motto is "amor es nuestro sazon" — love is our seasoning.
breakfast-house-west-town.descriptor: Family-owned breakfast and brunch spot on West Grand Ave

broadway-playhouse-at-water-tower-place.text: The original theater here opened in 1976, closed in 1983 and spent years as a cinema. Tony DeSantis then put $9 million into converting a nearby former movie theater into a live house, which reopened in May 2004 as Drury Lane Water Tower Place; Broadway In Chicago and the Nederlander Organization rebranded the 549-seat room the Broadway Playhouse in September 2010.
broadway-playhouse-at-water-tower-place.descriptor: 549-seat Broadway In Chicago theater on E. Chestnut by Water Tower Place

writtenFor.name: Broadway Playhouse at Water Tower Place

broken-shaker-chicago.text: Broken Shaker sits in the bar of the Freehand, a hostel-hotel inside a restored 1927 Art Deco building on Ohio Street, and builds its drinks around house syrups, infusions, garden herbs and fresh-pressed produce. Tales of the Cocktail named it Best American Hotel Bar.
broken-shaker-chicago.descriptor: Cocktail bar in the Freehand hotel, 19 E. Ohio St, River North

brunas.text: "Bella Bruna" Cani opened Bruna's in 1933, the year Prohibition ended, and was known to dance on the bar while the customers sang. The restaurant bills itself as Chicago's third-oldest Italian; Siena-born Luciano Silvestri bought it in 1981 after Bruna's health failed and kept her recipes, including the roast chicken served every Sunday.
brunas.descriptor: Italian restaurant on S. Oakley Ave. in Heart of Italy, open since 1933

bub-city.text: A Melman-family (Lettuce Entertain You) take on a country-western roadhouse: house-smoked brisket, ribs and pulled pork, more than 125 whiskeys, oysters and crab on ice, and live bands playing country covers. The decor leans all the way in, down to patriotic beer-can displays.
bub-city.descriptor: Honky-tonk barbecue bar with live country music at 435 N. Clark St

buckingham-fountain.text: Kate Sturges Buckingham gave the fountain to Chicago in 1927 as a memorial to her brother Clarence. Architect Edward H. Bennett modeled it on the Latona Fountain at Versailles, and its four sets of seahorses stand for the states bordering Lake Michigan: Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Wisconsin. The center jet throws water 150 feet, and the fountain opened Married... with Children.
buckingham-fountain.descriptor: Rococo fountain in Grant Park with a 150-foot center jet, given in 1927

buona.text: This Roosevelt Road stand is where Buona began: in 1981 Joe and Peggy Buonavolanto took a $10,000 second mortgage on their house half a mile away to open it. Peggy worked out the Italian beef recipe with help from her uncle "Junior," who ran Mr. Beef on Orleans Street. Their five sons grew it into the country's largest family-owned Italian beef group.
buona.descriptor: The original 1981 Buona Italian beef stand on Roosevelt Rd in Berwyn

buona-west-roosevelt-road.text: Buona is the Buonavolanto family's Italian beef chain, started in Berwyn in 1981 after they took a second mortgage on their house to open it. Peggy Buonavolanto worked out the beef recipe with help from her Uncle Junior, who ran Mr. Beef on Orleans Street — and it has stayed a family business across three generations.
buona-west-roosevelt-road.descriptor: Italian beef counter of a family chain founded in Berwyn in 1981

burnham-harbor.text: The harbor grew out of Daniel Burnham's 1909 Plan of Chicago, with the breakwater running the length of the park by 1924 and Northerly Island forming its outer edge. It now holds roughly 1,120 slips plus the Burnham Park Yacht Club, and the ancient Roman column Mussolini sent Chicago after Italo Balbo's 1933 transatlantic flight still stands nearby.
burnham-harbor.descriptor: 1,100-slip lakefront harbor beside Soldier Field and the Museum Campus

burnham-park.text: Burnham Park is the 598-acre, six-mile lakefront strip built largely on landfill and named in 1927 for Daniel Burnham, whose 1909 Plan of Chicago called for it. It hosted the 1933–34 Century of Progress world's fair, and its landforms include Northerly Island — the only offshore island in the Burnham Plan that actually got built — plus Promontory Point and 31st Street Beach.
burnham-park.descriptor: Six-mile lakefront park on landfill, Grant Park down to Jackson Park

burrito-beach.text: Burrito Beach has been a Chicago fast-casual fixture since 1995, building burritos and tacos from hand-carved, marinated meats that are char-grilled to order, with salsas and guacamole made daily. The small local chain has since spread to the Loop, Ogilvie station, hospital lobbies and O'Hare.
burrito-beach.descriptor: Fast-casual Cal-Mex counter on Ohio St. in Streeterville, local since 1995

burrito-house-irving-park.descriptor: Late-night taqueria on N. Elston Ave. serving burritos, tacos and nachos

burrito-house-lake-view.descriptor: Neighborhood taqueria in Lake View for burritos, tacos and Mexican plates

butch-mcguires.text: Butch McGuire borrowed money from his mother to open on Division Street in 1961 and became known as the unofficial mayor of the strip. The bar's own history calls it a premier singles bar and claims more than 10,000 marriages have come out of encounters there. Every winter it disappears under holiday decorations and double-decker model trains, with proceeds going to Mercy Home.
butch-mcguires.descriptor: Gold Coast saloon on Division Street since 1961, famed for Christmas decor

byline-bank-aragon-ballroom.text: Opened July 15, 1926, the Aragon was given an interior by theater architect John Eberson evoking the courtyard of a Moorish castle around a 21,000-square-foot dance floor. In its heyday crowds topping 18,000 a week danced here to nightly WGN broadcasts heard across the U.S., Canada and reportedly Britain; it's now a 5,000-capacity Live Nation venue, known as the Byline Bank Aragon since 2019.
byline-bank-aragon-ballroom.descriptor: 1926 Moorish-castle ballroom and concert hall in Uptown

byrons-hot-dogs.text: Byron's is a North Side hot dog counter on Irving Park Road, a block off the Wrigleyville stretch. Past the dogs it does Italian beef, sausages, chili dogs and gyros, its thin crispy fries have their own following, and the stand catered at the White House in 2010.
byrons-hot-dogs.descriptor: Chicago-style hot dog stand at 1017 W. Irving Park Rd.

writtenFor.name: Byron's Hot Dogs - Lake View East

byrons-hot-dogs-lake-view-east.text: Byron's does the full Chicago-style dog — mustard, chopped onion, neon relish, tomato, a pickle spear, sport peppers and celery salt on a poppy seed bun, and absolutely no ketchup — alongside Italian beef, sausages, chili dogs and gyros. Its thin, crisp fries have a following of their own, and Byron's catered at the White House in 2010.
byrons-hot-dogs-lake-view-east.descriptor: Chicago-style hot dog stand with thin crispy fries, Italian beef and gyros

cabra.text: Cabra — Spanish for "goat" — opened in 2019 on the roof of the Hoxton hotel at 200 N. Green Street, with a menu Stephanie Izard drew from her travels through Peru: ceviche, saltados, sticky wings and pisco sours over sweeping West Loop views. The Boka Restaurant Group spot took a Bib Gourmand in 2020 and Time Out Chicago's Best New Restaurant nod in 2019.
cabra.descriptor: Stephanie Izard's Peruvian rooftop restaurant atop the Hoxton in Fulton Market

cadillac-palace-theatre.text: It opened on Randolph Street in 1926 as the New Palace, a French Baroque vaudeville house designed by Rapp and Rapp. Its brass ornament was painted white during World War II so the government wouldn't requisition the metal; a $20 million restoration in 1999 uncovered it again. The 2,344-seat house now takes pre-Broadway tryouts, among them The Producers in 2001.
cadillac-palace-theatre.descriptor: 1926 Rapp & Rapp Loop theater on W. Randolph, now a Broadway touring house

cafe-ba-ba-reeba.text: Cafe Ba-Ba-Reeba! opened at 2024 N. Halsted in 1985 as Chicago's original tapas bar, a Lettuce Entertain You restaurant that introduced the city to small plates and pitchers of sangria. Four decades on it's still known for paella, croquetas and bacon-wrapped dates.
cafe-ba-ba-reeba.descriptor: Spanish tapas and paella on N. Halsted in Lincoln Park since 1985

cafe-mustache.text: Open on Milwaukee Ave. since 2010, Cafe Mustache pours locally roasted coffee through the afternoon and then flips at 6pm into a 21-and-over bar with live music, karaoke and DJ sets — the Chicago Reader has called it the city's best non-traditional music venue, and Newcity named its vegan chili the best in Chicago.
cafe-mustache.descriptor: Logan Square coffeehouse by day, 21+ bar and live music venue after 6pm

cafecito.descriptor: Cuban cafe known for pressed Cubano sandwiches and cafe con leche

cafecito-streeterville.text: A small Cuban counter on Congress Parkway in the Loop, next door to the Hostelling International hostel, best known for its Cubano — crusty toasted bread, juicy roast pork, thick pickles, mustard and gooey cheese — chased with a café con leche.
cafecito-streeterville.descriptor: Cuban café and Cubano sandwiches at 26 E Congress Pkwy in the Loop

caffe-umbria-river-north.text: Caffè Umbria is the Bizzarri family's coffee company — founded by third-generation master roaster Emanuele Bizzarri, drawing on an Italian coffee heritage that began in Perugia — with cafés in Seattle, Portland, Miami Beach and Chicago. The River North room sits in the historic John R. Thompson Building on Clark Street; the roastery and coffee lab are out on Armitage Ave.
caffe-umbria-river-north.descriptor: Italian espresso bar at 346 N. Clark in the historic John R. Thompson Building

california-clipper.text: The Clipper has poured since 1937, in a building that has stood at 1002 N California Ave since 1912, when it opened as the L.L. Freeman Theater. The red leather booths and vintage red light fixtures are part of its signature look; it closed temporarily during the pandemic and was revived, and live music — jazz, blues, funk, country, DJ sets — runs most nights.
california-clipper.descriptor: Post-Prohibition cocktail lounge on California Ave in Humboldt Park, live music

calo-ristorante.text: The Recchia family has run Calo on Clark Street since 1963, making it one of Andersonville's longest-running restaurants — six decades of stone-fired pizza, old-recipe pastas and the fall-off-the-bone ribs it is known for, served in a brick-walled room painted with Italian murals.
calo-ristorante.descriptor: Family-run Italian on N. Clark St in Andersonville since 1963

candelite.text: Reporter Monica Eng's history of Chicago tavern-style pizza — the thin, square-cut pie locals order more than deep dish — names the Candlelite in Rogers Park as one of a handful of spots that could have originated the style, which she dates to roughly 1946–1950.
candelite.descriptor: Thin-crust tavern-style pizza spot in Rogers Park

carmines.text: A Gold Coast fixture on the Rush Street strip, Carmine's belongs to Alex Dana's Rosebud Restaurant Group and trades in old-school Italian — handmade pasta, generous portions built for a table. It reopened in January 2026 after a $4 million rebuild, and added an all-weather second-floor terrace overlooking the Gold Coast that June.
carmines.descriptor: Rush Street Italian restaurant from the Rosebud group, with a second-floor terrace

carnitas-uruapan-restaurant.text: Inocencio Carbajal, known as "El Guero," opened Carnitas Uruapan in 1975, cooking pork the way it's done in Uruapan, Michoacán. The Pilsen shop at 1725 W. 18th St. is takeout-only and built around one thing — carnitas. The family has since added Gage Park and Little Village locations.
carnitas-uruapan-restaurant.descriptor: Michoacán-style pork carnitas counter on 18th St in Pilsen since 1975

writtenFor.name: Carnitas Uruapan Restaurant - Lower West Side

carnitas-uruapan-restaurant-gage-park.text: Inocencio Carbajal, known as "El Guero," opened Carnitas Uruapan in Pilsen in 1975, cooking pork the way it's done in Uruapan, Michoacan. The menu stays short — carnitas, tacos dorados, tacos de carnitas — and unlike the takeout-only Pilsen original, the Gage Park shop on 55th Street has a dining room.
carnitas-uruapan-restaurant-gage-park.descriptor: Michoacan-style carnitas at 2813 W. 55th St.; family-run since 1975

carnivale.text: Carnivale is one of Jerry Kleiner's splashy West Loop rooms — a 400-seat blast of color on Fulton Market built for noise, mojitos and margaritas, with grilled skirt steak and ropa vieja among the Latin American plates it is known for.
carnivale.descriptor: Big, colorful Latin American restaurant on Fulton Market in the West Loop

carousel.text: The carousel turns in Pier Park at Navy Pier alongside the Centennial Wheel, the teacups and the Wave Swinger. The original ride ran from the pier's 1995 reopening until a cold-weather mechanical failure in early 2019; the replacement installed that summer had previously spun at Dorney Park in Pennsylvania.
carousel.descriptor: Carousel ride in Pier Park at Navy Pier

carsons-ribs.text: Dean Carson, a third-generation Chicagoan from a family that had been in food and beverage since the 1930s, opened Carson's in 1977 on a promise of large portions of great food at an honest price, built around baby back ribs in the house barbecue sauce. It still advertises itself as 'America's #1 Barbecue' and has added outposts in Deerfield and Milwaukee.
carsons-ribs.descriptor: Barbecue rib house at 465 E Illinois St in Streeterville, since 1977

centennial-wheel.text: Named for Navy Pier's 100th anniversary, the Centennial Wheel debuted May 27, 2016 to replace the pier's 1995 Ferris wheel — 46 feet taller at 196 feet, with a twelve-minute ride of three full revolutions in enclosed, climate-controlled gondolas. It's a Dutch Wheels DW60, the first of its kind in the United States, built to take 115 mph winds.
centennial-wheel.descriptor: 196-foot Ferris wheel with enclosed gondolas at Navy Pier

ceres-cafe.text: Ceres sits in the lobby of the Chicago Board of Trade Building at 141 W. Jackson and takes its name from the Roman goddess of agriculture whose statue crowns the building. It opened as the Broker's Inn in 1967, took the Ceres name in December 1989, and has been a commodities traders' haunt ever since — famous enough for its punishing pours that it lent its name to a first-season episode of The Bear.
ceres-cafe.descriptor: Bar and diner in the Board of Trade lobby, known for heavy pours

cesars-killer-margaritas.descriptor: Mexican restaurant on N Broadway in Lakeview built around its house margaritas

charles-wacker.text: Charles H. Wacker (1856–1929), a brewing and malting executive turned civic booster, chaired the Chicago Plan Commission from 1909 to 1926 and spent those years selling Burnham's Plan of Chicago to the public through speeches, press coverage and Wacker's Manual of the Plan of Chicago. Wacker Drive carries his name, and he's buried here in Graceland, the 1860 cemetery nicknamed the "Cemetery of Architects."
charles-wacker.descriptor: Grave in Graceland Cemetery of the man Wacker Drive is named for

chengdu-impression.text: The Lincoln Park room is part of a small local Sichuan group that also runs Chengdu Impression kitchens in Wicker Park, Edgewater and Logan Square, plus a Chinatown sister restaurant, Dongpo Impression.
chengdu-impression.descriptor: Sichuan restaurant at 2545 N Halsted in Lincoln Park

chester-howlin-wolf-burnett.text: This bronze plaque is part of the Bronzeville Walk of Fame, which honors notable residents of Chicago's historic Black Metropolis. Howlin' Wolf came north from Mississippi in late 1952 at Leonard Chess's urging, put together a new band with guitarist Hubert Sumlin, and cut "Smokestack Lightning" and "Spoonful" here.
chester-howlin-wolf-burnett.descriptor: Bronze plaque on the Bronzeville Walk of Fame in Chicago's Black Metropolis

chicago-architecture-center.text: Founded in 1966 as the Chicago School of Architecture Foundation — originally to save H.H. Richardson's Glessner House — it was renamed the Chicago Architecture Foundation in 1979 and moved into Mies van der Rohe's One Illinois Center on the river in 2018. Its centerpiece is the Chicago Model, a 3-D printed scale model of the central city, and it runs the docent-led architecture river cruise and Open House Chicago, the city's largest annual architecture event.
chicago-architecture-center.descriptor: Architecture museum on the Chicago River with a 3-D scale model of the city

chicago-avenue-pumping-station.text: Built in 1869 by William W. Boyington, architect of the Water Tower across the street, the station still pumps Lake Michigan water for the city. In the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 its roof caught fire and collapsed into the pumps, destroying them — and with them any hope of enough water to stop the blaze. Much of the interior was converted to the Lookingglass Theatre in 2003–04.
chicago-avenue-pumping-station.descriptor: 1869 limestone pumping station facing the Old Water Tower on Michigan Ave

chicago-childrens-museum.text: The Junior League of Chicago founded the museum in 1982 in response to programming cutbacks in the Chicago Public Schools, starting it inside the Chicago Public Library. It moved to Navy Pier in 1995, and a 2006 plan to relocate to Grant Park drew neighborhood opposition and was rejected by the Park District in 2011; the museum then signed a 90-year Navy Pier lease in late 2012.
chicago-childrens-museum.descriptor: Hands-on children's museum at Navy Pier since 1995

chicago-chop-house.text: The Chop House occupies a Victorian brownstone built in 1897 on Ontario Street in River North, and bills itself as the only steakhouse in Chicago devoted exclusively to USDA Prime and better, with every cut hand-butchered in house.
chicago-chop-house.descriptor: Prime-only steakhouse in an 1897 brownstone at 60 W. Ontario, River North

chicago-cultural-center.text: Built in 1897 as Chicago's central public library and a Grand Army of the Republic memorial hall, the building became the nation's first free municipal cultural center in 1978. Preston Bradley Hall's 38-foot Tiffany glass dome, made of more than 60,000 pieces of glass, is billed as the largest in the world, and there's a second stained-glass dome by Healy and Millet. Admission is still free.
chicago-cultural-center.descriptor: Free city arts venue in the 1897 former public library, 78 E. Washington

chicago-cut-steakhouse.text: Chicago Cut sits at the foot of 300 N. LaSalle, the 2009 Pickard Chilton tower whose half-acre waterfront garden runs right to the river's edge — diners can pull up by boat and dock at the door. It's a deal-making room that opens at 7 a.m. weekdays for the downtown power-breakfast crowd.
chicago-cut-steakhouse.descriptor: Riverfront steakhouse at 300 N LaSalle with boat docking and 7am breakfast

chicago-french-market.text: Opened in 2009 by the Bensidoun family, the largest market operator in and around Paris since 1953, it sits in MetraMarket one level below the Ogilvie Transportation Center, between Randolph and Washington. More than 30 hand-picked local vendors make it a year-round, permanent indoor marketplace.
chicago-french-market.descriptor: Year-round indoor food hall with 30+ vendors under Ogilvie Transportation Center

chicago-harbor.text: Chicago Harbor is the breakwater-ringed water at the river's mouth: DuSable and Monroe harbors, the Chicago Yacht Club, the Coast Guard station and the Chicago Harbor Lock all sit inside it. Its entrance is marked by the Chicago Harbor Lighthouse, built in 1893 for the World's Columbian Exposition and moved out to the breakwater in 1919.
chicago-harbor.descriptor: Breakwater harbor at the mouth of the Chicago River, off Navy Pier

chicago-history-museum.text: Founded in 1856 as the Chicago Historical Society, it lost its original collection — including Lincoln's final draft of the Emancipation Proclamation — in the Great Chicago Fire, and adopted its current public name in 2006. Its roughly 22 million holdings include Lincoln's deathbed and the table on which Lee signed his 1865 surrender to Grant.
chicago-history-museum.descriptor: Lincoln Park museum of Chicago history at Clark and North Ave

chicago-pizza-and-oven-grinder-co.text: Open since 1972, it serves a "pizza pot pie" — Sicilian dough baked upside down over sauce and cheese in a bowl, then flipped at your table. The garage across Clark Street was the site of the 1929 St. Valentine's Day Massacre, and legend says this building was a lookout for Capone's gunmen, though there's no evidence for it.
chicago-pizza-and-oven-grinder-co.descriptor: Lincoln Park pizza spot since 1972, known for its upside-down pizza pot pie

writtenFor.name: Chicago Pizza and Oven Grinder Co.

chicago-riverwalk.text: A pedestrian walkway on the south bank of the Chicago River's main branch, begun with the 2001 Wacker Drive reconstruction and expanded in phases through 2016. The expansion laid out six "rooms" — Marina Plaza, the Cove, River Theater, Water Plaza, the Jetty, the Boardwalk — with floating wetland gardens, fishing piers and amphitheater steps down to the water.
chicago-riverwalk.descriptor: Public promenade along the Chicago River's main branch downtown

chicago-shakespeare-theater.text: Barbara Gaines founded the company in 1986 as a workshop staging Shakespeare on the roof of a Lincoln Park pub. It opened its purpose-built Navy Pier home in 1999, built around a 510-seat Courtyard Theater whose thrust stage wraps the audience close on three sides. The company won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 2008 and added The Yard, a reconfigurable 150-to-850-seat space, in 2017.
chicago-shakespeare-theater.descriptor: Navy Pier theater with a courtyard thrust stage, founded 1986

chicago-theatre.text: Rapp & Rapp built it as the flagship of the Balaban & Katz chain, promoted as the "Wonder Theatre of the World"; it opened in 1921 with films, stage shows and a 26-rank Wurlitzer organ, and seats about 3,600. The vertical CHICAGO sign, hung with the Y-shaped municipal device that stands for the forked Chicago River, has become an unofficial emblem of the city.
chicago-theatre.descriptor: 1921 State Street movie palace with the landmark CHICAGO marquee

chicago-union-station.text: Completed in 1925 from a Daniel Burnham plan and finished by Graham, Anderson, Probst & White after his death, its Great Hall sits under a barrel-vaulted skylight 115 feet up. The travertine staircase is where Brian De Palma shot the baby-carriage shootout in The Untouchables (1987).
chicago-union-station.descriptor: 1925 Beaux-Arts rail terminal in the West Loop with a soaring Great Hall

chicago-waffles-near-south-side.text: The South Loop branch of a local breakfast mini-chain that has grown to five locations around Chicago in more than 14 years. Waffles are the point: the loaded "Chicago's Waffles Best" piled with vanilla ice cream, strawberries, blueberries, chocolate chips, walnuts and caramel, plus chicken-and-waffle plates and a Dubai-chocolate waffle.
chicago-waffles-near-south-side.descriptor: Belgian-waffle breakfast house at 1400 S Michigan Ave, South Loop

chicago-water-tower.text: Built in 1869 to William W. Boyington's design in yellowing Lemont limestone, it was the only public building in the burned zone to survive the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 — though its roof, not made of limestone, caught fire and the pumps stopped working. It now holds the City Gallery, a free photography space run by the city's tourism office.
chicago-water-tower.descriptor: 1869 limestone tower on Michigan Ave, now a free city art gallery

chicagos-home-of-chicken-waffles.text: Tonya and Darnell Johnson opened this Oak Park dining room at 543 Madison St. in 2010, the second location of their Bronzeville original. Tonya traces the chicken-and-waffles pairing to 1920s jazz-club crowds who spilled out in the small hours and couldn't decide between breakfast and dinner. The kitchen also turns out catfish, the five-egg omelet, peach cobbler and banana pudding.
chicagos-home-of-chicken-waffles.descriptor: Soul food and chicken-and-waffles house on Madison St in Oak Park since 2010

chicagos-pizza-old-irving-park.descriptor: Neighborhood pizzeria on West Irving Park Road in Irving Park

chief-oneills-pub-restaurant.text: It carries the name of Francis O'Neill, Chicago's police superintendent from 1901 to 1905 and, in his biographer Nicholas Carolan's words, the greatest individual influence on the evolution of Irish traditional dance music in the twentieth century — he recruited Irish musicians onto the force and published O'Neill's Music of Ireland, 1,850 pieces, in 1903. The pub displays memorabilia tied to him.
chief-oneills-pub-restaurant.descriptor: Avondale Irish pub named for Chicago police chief Francis O'Neill

chilam-balam.text: Chef Chuy Valencia — then 23 and fresh out of Rick Bayless's Frontera and Topolobampo kitchens by way of Adobo Grill — opened Chilam Balam in a cramped subterranean room in late August 2009, and the Reader singled it out in a crowded neo-Mexican field. It remains a cash-only BYOB built on Mexican shared plates and seasonal specials.
chilam-balam.descriptor: Subterranean BYOB Mexican small-plates spot on N Broadway in Lakeview

cho-sun-ok-restaurant.text: Cho Sun Ok has held the corner of Lincoln and Berteau in North Center since 1980. Time Out's advice is to talk the server into letting you cook the sliced beef yourself at the table rather than have it done in the kitchen — it comes out more tender — and to work through the long spread of banchan side dishes.
cho-sun-ok-restaurant.descriptor: Old-school Korean BBQ at Lincoln and Berteau, tabletop grills, since 1980

chopin-theatre.text: The building opened in 1918 as a nickelodeon designed by Worthmann & Steinbach and cycled through names — the Harding in 1926, then the Pix by 1948. Polish immigrant Zygmunt Dyrkacz bought the derelict theater in 1990 and reopened it; it now runs two stages (226 and 175 seats) and has presented more than 2,100 theater, literature, music, dance and film events with artists from 49 countries.
chopin-theatre.descriptor: 1918 Wicker Park movie house, now a two-stage theater on Division St

cibc-theatre.text: It opened in 1906 as the Majestic Theatre, a vaudeville house designed by Edmund R. Krause with the Rapp brothers, running a dozen-plus acts a day. Now an 1,800-seat Broadway In Chicago venue, it has cycled through names — Shubert, LaSalle Bank, Bank of America, PrivateBank, then CIBC in 2017 — and hosted the Chicago sit-down of Hamilton from 2016 to 2020.
cibc-theatre.descriptor: 1,800-seat Loop Broadway house that opened in 1906 as the Majestic Theatre

city-winery.text: Michael Dorf opened the first City Winery in New York in 2008 and brought the format to Chicago's West Loop in 2012: wine actually made and barreled on the premises, a Mediterranean-leaning restaurant, and a ticketed stage running rock, blues, jazz, R&B and comedy.
city-winery.descriptor: Working urban winery and seated concert venue at 1200 W. Randolph

civic-opera-house.text: Utilities magnate Samuel Insull built this 1929 Art Deco house, whose silhouette is seen as a huge chair — earning the nickname "Insull's Throne." It opened on November 4, 1929, days after the stock market crash. The 3,276-seat auditorium has been home to the Lyric Opera of Chicago since 1954, and the Joffrey Ballet since 2021.
civic-opera-house.descriptor: Art Deco opera house at 20 N Wacker, home of the Lyric Opera

club-lago.text: Gus and Ida Lazzerini opened Club Lago in 1952 to feed printers and paper salesmen in Smokey Hollow, the warehouse district around Superior Street. Three generations of the same family still run it, and the tin ceiling, old back bars and terrazzo floor are still there.
club-lago.descriptor: Family-run Northern Italian restaurant and bar in River North since 1952

club-lucky.text: The room drew Polish regulars in the years after Prohibition before it became a supper club, and it has been restored to a 1950s cocktail-culture look. The food is old-school family-style Italian — grilled calamari, chicken Vesuvio, escarole with sausage and beans — with signature martinis and classic standards playing at night.
club-lucky.descriptor: Italian supper club on Wabansia in Wicker Park — martinis and chicken Vesuvio

coalfire.text: Coalfire's Valoriani brick oven burns clean coal at around 1,500 degrees, turning out blistered, leopard-spotted thin crust in under two minutes. Chicago Magazine voted it the #1 best pizza in Chicago.
coalfire.descriptor: Coal-oven thin-crust pizza at 1321 W. Grand Ave in West Town

coalfire-west-town.text: Thin, blistered, leopard-spotted pies come out of a Valoriani brick oven fired with coal at 1,500 degrees, baked in under two minutes. The Grand Avenue shop in West Town came first; this is the larger Lakeview outpost at 3707 N Southport.
coalfire-west-town.descriptor: Coal-oven thin-crust pizzeria on N Southport in Lakeview

coco-pazzo.text: Jack Weiss opened Coco Pazzo in 1992 in a Hubbard Street loft building more than a hundred years old, serving the straightforward seasonal cooking of Tuscany. The room — timber beams, brick walls, cypress floors, an antique bar and blue velvet drapes for privacy — has been a River North special-occasion table for three decades.
coco-pazzo.descriptor: Tuscan restaurant in a century-old River North loft, open since 1992

colectivo-coffee.text: Colectivo started in Milwaukee in 1993 as Alterra Coffee Roasters, taking its current name in 2013 from the funky buses used for public transit across Latin America. It crossed the state line in 2017 with its first Chicago shops in Lincoln Park and Logan Square; the coffee is still roasted in Milwaukee.
colectivo-coffee.descriptor: Milwaukee roaster's cafe at 2530 N Clark in Lincoln Park

columbus-park.text: Jens Jensen began designing Columbus Park in 1915 and it was largely finished by 1920 — the 135-acre Prairie School landscape widely considered his masterwork, with stone waterfalls, a council ring and native plantings that were rare for the time. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2003.
columbus-park.descriptor: Jens Jensen's 135-acre prairie-style park in Austin, with waterfalls and council ring

comiskey-park-home-plate.text: Comiskey Park — christened the "Baseball Palace of the World" — stood on West 35th Street in Armour Square from 1910 to 1990, hosting four World Series, three All-Star Games, Joe Louis's 1937 title win over James J. Braddock, and 1979's Disco Demolition Night. After the 1991 demolition, the footprint became a parking lot: a marble plaque marks the exact spot of home plate, with the old foul lines painted across the asphalt.
comiskey-park-home-plate.descriptor: Marble home-plate marker in Rate Field's lot, where old Comiskey stood

connies-pizza.text: In 1963 Jim Stolfe traded his Oldsmobile Starfire for a small storefront pizzeria on 26th Street on the South Side. It already carried the previous owner's name, and by the time he could afford to change the sign, Connie's had stuck. The family business later moved to its big Archer Avenue flagship and built a deep-dish empire from there.
connies-pizza.descriptor: Deep-dish pizza institution at 2373 S. Archer Ave on the South Side since 1963

connies-pizza-armour-square.text: Connie's has been making Chicago deep dish on Archer Avenue since 1963. The Near South Side room is built for volume — it seats up to 400, with ample parking — and sits just minutes from the Loop.
connies-pizza-armour-square.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria on S. Archer Ave, since 1963

conte-di-savolia.text: One of the last real Italian groceries left on Taylor Street, Conte Di Savoia has sold subs, house-made pasta, pastries and imported Italian goods since 1948. Michael Dicosola bought it in the early 1980s and now runs it with his two sons, who manage its two shops. The surrounding Little Italy lost roughly 200 Italian businesses and 800 homes to UIC's 1963 expansion, with the Eisenhower Expressway cutting further into the neighborhood.
conte-di-savolia.descriptor: Little Italy Italian deli and grocery on Taylor Street since 1948

contemporary.text: These galleries sit inside the Art Institute's Modern Wing, the 264,000-square-foot Renzo Piano addition that opened in May 2009 and made the Art Institute the second-largest art museum in the United States after the Met. The wing holds European modernism, art from 1960 onward, photography, design and architecture, and its Nichols Bridgeway carries you from the rooftop sculpture garden into Millennium Park.
contemporary.descriptor: Contemporary art galleries in the Art Institute's Renzo Piano Modern Wing

coq-dor.text: The Drake's lower-level lounge dates to the end of Prohibition — the hotel says Coq d'Or was the second establishment in Chicago to be granted a liquor license once drinking was legal again. It has stayed the same kind of room ever since: small, intimate and sultry, built for live jazz, cocktails and hushed conversation.
coq-dor.descriptor: Wood-paneled piano bar in the lower level of the Drake Hotel

couch-tomb.text: Hotelier Ira Couch, who ran the Tremont House with his brother James, was entombed here eighteen months after his 1857 death, back when this ground was Chicago's City Cemetery. From the 1860s the city moved the bodies elsewhere and turned the land into Lincoln Park — but the Couch mausoleum, designed by John M. Van Osdel, stayed put. It is the only marked grave left there.
couch-tomb.descriptor: 1850s stone mausoleum in Lincoln Park, the last grave left from City Cemetery

court-theatre.text: Founded in 1955, Court is the University of Chicago's professional theater company, staging four plays a season at 5535 S. Ellis Ave. for more than 35,000 people a year. In 2022 it won the Regional Theatre Tony Award, one of the most prestigious honors for a theater outside New York.
court-theatre.descriptor: Classic-repertory theater on the U. of Chicago campus in Hyde Park

cozy-corner-belmont-gardens.descriptor: Diner and pancake house at 4356 W Diversey Ave on the Northwest Side

credit-union-1-arena.text: Opened in 1982 as the UIC Pavilion and renamed in 2018 under a Credit Union 1 naming-rights deal, the Skidmore, Owings and Merrill-designed arena seats about 8,000 for basketball and 10,300 for concerts. Home court for UIC Flames basketball, it also housed the WNBA's Chicago Sky from 2006 to 2009 — and in March 2016 a Donald Trump rally here was called off amid unrest between protesters and supporters.
credit-union-1-arena.descriptor: UIC's campus arena on S Racine, home of the Flames since 1982

crisp.text: Crisp is chef-owner Jae Lee's mash-up of his Korean upbringing with American fried chicken — an idea, the shop says, his mother warned would ruin a thousand years of tradition. It comes as wings, a whole bird or a sandwich, with kimchi, Buddha bowls and Superfly frites alongside.
crisp.descriptor: Korean fried chicken shop on N. Broadway in Lakeview

crown-fountain.text: Jaume Plensa's 2004 fountain sets two 50-foot glass-block towers facing each other across a shallow black granite reflecting pool. Each plays video portraits of about 1,000 Chicago residents in random rotation, and water appears to spout from the mouths of the projected faces — a modern take on the gargoyle fountain.
crown-fountain.descriptor: Millennium Park video fountain with 50-foot glass-block towers

cruz-blanca-brewery-taqueria.text: Rick Bayless and partner Manny Valdes opened Cruz Blanca in 2016 next door to Leña Brava, pairing a wood-fired taquería with a working brewery. Bayless walked away from both Randolph Street rooms in July 2020 after the partnership soured, leaving Valdes in full control; the brewpub kept going at 904 W. Randolph on tlayudas, wood-grilled tacos and house-brewed Mexican-style lagers.
cruz-blanca-brewery-taqueria.descriptor: Mexican brewpub on the West Loop's Randolph St: wood-fired tacos, house beer

cubby-bear.text: Established in 1953 at Addison and Clark across from Wrigley Field, the Cubby Bear is a game-day institution that doubles as a rock club — it built a name on rock and punk bookings, and its stage has hosted Johnny Cash and B.B. King as well as Dave Matthews Band and No Doubt.
cubby-bear.descriptor: Sports bar and rock club across from Wrigley Field since 1953

dagostinos-pizza-and-pub-wrigleyville.text: D'Agostino's sits at 1351 W. Addison, a few blocks west of Wrigley Field, and turns out the cracker-thin, tavern-cut Chicago pie the Reader has used as a reference point for the style. Its sidewalk patio wraps the corner from Addison onto Southport, which makes it a standard stop on Cubs days.
dagostinos-pizza-and-pub-wrigleyville.descriptor: Tavern-cut thin-crust pizza and beer at Addison & Southport, Wrigleyville

daisies.text: Chef Joe Frillman opened Daisies in June 2017 and cooks the Midwest as though it were a region of Italy — house-made pasta built on vegetables from his brother Tim's 30-acre farm in Prairie View, with meat used as an accent and kitchen scraps composted back to the farm. It holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand and Green Star, and moved to a larger Milwaukee Avenue space in 2023.
daisies.descriptor: Midwest-meets-Italy pasta restaurant on Milwaukee Ave in Logan Square

daleys-restaurant.text: Daley's has fed Woodlawn since 1892, when Irish immigrant John Daley started selling meals to construction workers; the Zee family has run it since 1918. It became Chicago's oldest restaurant when Schaller's Pump closed in 2017, and after 126 years at 809 E. 63rd St. it moved into the new Woodlawn Station development at 63rd and Cottage Grove, still serving breakfast and soul food.
daleys-restaurant.descriptor: Woodlawn soul food and breakfast diner, serving since 1892

dark-matter-coffee-the-mothership.text: Dark Matter has been roasting since 2007, when it started on Chicago's West Side at Star Lounge Coffee Bar, and it bills itself as "Interplanetary Dealers of Funky Coffee," putting out limited-run roasts made with musicians and artists. The Mothership is one of its Chicago cafes; Star Lounge, at 2521 W. Chicago Ave. in Ukrainian Village, remains the flagship.
dark-matter-coffee-the-mothership.descriptor: Chicago cafe from the Dark Matter Coffee roasting company

david-and-alfred-smart-museum-of-art.text: The Smart opened in 1974 as the University of Chicago's art museum, named for David and Alfred Smart, the Chicago brothers who published Esquire. Admission is free, and the collection of more than 17,000 objects spans Asian, European, modern and contemporary art — including Picasso, Rothko and Rivera, plus the original dining room furniture Frank Lloyd Wright designed for the nearby Robie House.
david-and-alfred-smart-museum-of-art.descriptor: Free University of Chicago art museum in Hyde Park

writtenFor.name: David and Alfred Smart Museum of Art

delilahs.text: A rock-and-roll bar at 2771 N. Lincoln Ave. that pours an enormous whiskey list alongside more than 300 beers, with DJs spinning punk and classic rock Sunday through Thursday and the jukebox in customers' hands on weekends. It is open 365 days a year, and tastings are a regular fixture.
delilahs.descriptor: Rock-and-roll dive bar on N. Lincoln Ave with a huge whiskey list

demera-ethiopian-restaurant.text: Chef-owner Tigist Reda's Uptown room serves injera-lined messob combination platters, fried sambussas and house-made honey wine (t'ej). Reda, who was born in Tigray, has raised more than $100,000 for women displaced by the war there, and she is planning a much bigger Demera — a 7,000-square-foot dining room with rooftop space — at 4528 S. Cottage Grove Ave. in Bronzeville.

devil-dawgs.text: Devil Dawgs is a homegrown chain that opened its first storefront in Lincoln Park in 2010 and now runs six shops around Chicago and Evanston. Beyond the classic Chicago dog on a natural-casing Vienna Beef frank, it's known for the jumbo spicy sausage the place is named after, Italian beef, and a vegan Chicago-style dog.
devil-dawgs.descriptor: Chicago-style Vienna Beef hot dogs and Italian beef, South Loop location

devil-dawgs-chicago-loop.text: Devil Dawgs started in 2010 in Lincoln Park a few steps from DePaul, following in the footsteps of the iconic Demon Dogs, with the stated aim of bringing the great Chicago-style hot dog and fries back to the neighborhood. It has since grown to seven spots, including this one on Milwaukee Avenue in Wicker Park.
devil-dawgs-chicago-loop.descriptor: Chicago-style hot dogs and burgers on Milwaukee Ave in Wicker Park

dimos-logan-square.text: Founder Dimitri Syrkin-Nikolau built Dimo's around oddball slices: the best seller is The Mac, a pizza topped with macaroni and cheese, next to things like The Reuben, made with house-made corned beef and sauerkraut. He has described the by-the-slice shops as "edgy and in your face."
dimos-logan-square.descriptor: By-the-slice pizza counter known for The Mac, a mac-and-cheese-topped pie

do-rite-donuts.descriptor: Donut, breakfast-sandwich and chicken-sandwich counter, made fresh all day

do-rite-donuts-chicken.text: Do-Rite makes its donuts, breakfast sandwiches and fried chicken sandwiches fresh through the day — old-fashioneds, a puffy cinnamon crunch and the crowd-drawing bacon donut. The Loop shop at 50 W. Randolph is a tiny morning-only spot that closes when it sells out; the small chain operates under Lettuce Entertain You.
do-rite-donuts-chicken.descriptor: Donut and fried-chicken-sandwich counter, part of a small Chicago chain

don-pedro-carnitas.text: Cooks stir giant brass vats of pig parts with paddles behind the counter, and the Sunday-morning pork rush backs the line up into the kitchen. The Chicago Reader has counted Carnitas Don Pedro among the city's "big three" carnitas houses alongside Carnitas Uruapan and Carnitas Don Rafa; birria, barbacoa, menudo and brain tacos fill out the rest of the counter.
don-pedro-carnitas.descriptor: Carnitas specialist on 18th Street in Pilsen

doughnut-vault.text: Restaurateur Brendan Sodikoff runs Doughnut Vault out of a chandeliered vestibule that holds roughly four people. It bakes a fixed batch each morning — around 750 doughnuts, buttermilk old-fashioned and chestnut-glazed among them — and shuts the window once they're gone, which is why the line down Franklin Street is part of the ritual.
doughnut-vault.descriptor: Tiny walk-up doughnut window on N Franklin St in River North

douglass-anna-and-frederick-park.text: William Le Baron Jenney laid this park out starting in 1869, raising the marshy ground with sand and manure hauled from the Union Stock Yards; his stone bridge and lagoon are still there, and Jens Jensen added prairie-style gardens after becoming superintendent in 1905. Long named for Senator Stephen A. Douglas, it was renamed in 2020 for abolitionist Frederick Douglass and his wife, Anna Murray Douglass.
douglass-anna-and-frederick-park.descriptor: 173-acre West Side park with a lagoon; home of Riot Fest

doves-luncheonette.text: The One Off Hospitality team behind Big Star opened Dove's on September 22, 2014, taking over the shuttered Cipollina storefront a few doors up Damen Avenue. It's a retro counter diner: Southern-inspired Mexican cooking, mezcal-heavy drinks, and records spinning all day.
doves-luncheonette.descriptor: Wicker Park counter diner: Southern-Mexican plates, mezcal, vinyl records

draftkings-sportsbook-at-wrigley-field.text: DraftKings opened this venue attached to Wrigley Field in June 2023 and began taking in-person bets there in March 2024, a rarity at a big-league ballpark. Citing Illinois's escalating betting taxes — plus Chicago's own levy — DraftKings shut the retail sportsbook on May 31, 2026. The space stays open as a bar and restaurant, but no longer takes wagers.
draftkings-sportsbook-at-wrigley-field.descriptor: Sports bar attached to Wrigley Field; took bets from 2024 to 2026

duck-duck-goat.text: Stephanie Izard — the first woman to win Top Chef — runs this Chinese-American restaurant, with hand-pulled noodles, house-made dumplings and BBQ ribs in a room styled as an 'everytown Chinatown.' It's her third restaurant with Boka Restaurant Group, after Girl & the Goat, and its signature crab rangoon goes back to a childhood favorite of hers.
duck-duck-goat.descriptor: Stephanie Izard's Chinese-American restaurant in the West Loop

duke-of-perth.text: Jack Crombie and his partners opened this Scottish tavern in 1989, and it spent 35 years at 2913 N. Clark, long enough for the Lakeview East chamber to pick it as a site for one of the city's first curbside cafes out front. It served its final day on Clark in May 2024 and moved a five-minute walk away to 2827 N. Broadway, the former Renaldi's Pizza.
duke-of-perth.descriptor: Scottish pub in Lakeview, open since 1989

dusable-black-history-museum-and-educati.text: Chartered on February 16, 1961 by Margaret Taylor-Burroughs, her husband Charles and others, it started in their own home as the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art before moving to Washington Park in 1973. It is the nation's oldest museum of African American culture, holds some 13,000 artifacts, and is named for Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, Chicago's first non-Native permanent settler.
dusable-black-history-museum-and-educati.descriptor: Washington Park museum of Black history and culture, founded in 1961

writtenFor.name: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center

ebenezer-missionary-baptist-church.text: Dankmar Adler — Louis Sullivan's partner — designed this Grand Boulevard building in 1899 as the Isaiah Temple synagogue; the Black Ebenezer congregation bought it in 1921 as the neighborhood changed. The first gospel chorus was formed here in 1931 under Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye, and the church's music nurtured Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin and Dinah Washington.
ebenezer-missionary-baptist-church.descriptor: 1899 Grand Boulevard church built as a synagogue by architect Dankmar Adler

ed-debevics.text: Rich Melman and Lee Cohn opened Ed Debevic's in 1984 around a fictional backstory: Ed, a Korean War vet, ran the joint. The gimmick is servers who insult you and put on choreographed numbers. The original Wells Street building in River North was demolished in 2015, and the diner reopened in Streeterville in 2021.
ed-debevics.descriptor: 1950s-style diner with wisecracking servers on E Ohio St, Streeterville, since 1984

el-che-steakhouse-bar.text: Everything at John Manion's West Loop restaurant is cooked over live fire in the Argentine asado tradition, with a dry-aging program and a South American wine list to match. Manion, whose group also runs Brasero, is enough of a fire evangelist that he co-authored a zine on backyard fire cooking.
el-che-steakhouse-bar.descriptor: Open-fire asado steakhouse at 845 W. Washington Blvd.

el-ideas.text: Phillip Foss opened EL Ideas in 2011 at 2419 W. 14th St., on a residential block near Douglass Park, and it won its first Michelin star in the 2014 Chicago guide. Diners eat a fixed multi-course BYOB menu, and the cook who actually made a dish is the one who walks out to introduce it — a touch the makers of "The Menu" said they borrowed for the film.
el-ideas.descriptor: Michelin-starred BYOB tasting menu on a residential block near Douglass Park

elis-cheesecake.text: Eli Schulman, who ran Eli's The Place for Steak, developed the cream-cheese-and-shortbread recipe in the late 1970s and sold it at the first Taste of Chicago in 1980, where it became the festival's signature dessert. The company moved to this 62,000-square-foot Dunning bakery in 1996 and has baked inaugural cakes for Bill Clinton and Barack Obama.
elis-cheesecake.descriptor: Cheesecake bakery and café in Dunning, on the Northwest Side

elske.text: Chefs David and Anna Posey opened Elske on Randolph Street's restaurant row in December 2016. Bon Appétit ranked it the No. 2 best new restaurant in America in 2017, and it earned a Michelin star in the 2018 Chicago guide.
elske.descriptor: Danish-inspired New American tasting menu on Randolph St, West Loop

ema.text: Lettuce Entertain You opened Ema in River North in June 2016 with chef partner CJ Jacobson, whose menu applies a light, California style of cooking to Mediterranean food. It is built around mezze — hummus in several versions, house-made labneh, spreads and vegetables — plus kebabs and grilled branzino. The name has since spread to Glenview and Austin, Texas.
ema.descriptor: Mediterranean mezze and kebabs by chef CJ Jacobson, 74 W Illinois St

emmett-till-mamie-till-mobley-house.text: This brick two-flat in West Woodlawn was home to Emmett Till and his mother Mamie Till-Mobley in the 1950s, before the 14-year-old's 1955 murder in Mississippi became one of the defining moments of the civil rights movement. It was named a Chicago Landmark in 2021 on the application of the nonprofit Blacks in Green, which now runs it as the Till House Museum.
emmett-till-mamie-till-mobley-house.descriptor: West Woodlawn two-flat where Emmett Till lived, now the Till House Museum

emporium-arcade-bar.text: Brothers Doug and Danny Marks opened the first Emporium in 2012, pairing craft beer with walls of arcade cabinets. The Logan Square outpost followed in 2014 at 2363 N Milwaukee — fewer cabinets than the Wicker Park original but far more room, with pool tables, air hockey, skeeball and miniature bowling, and a decommissioned food truck parked inside that hosts rotating chefs and vendors.
emporium-arcade-bar.descriptor: Logan Square arcade bar with pool, air hockey, skeeball and mini bowling

emporium-west-town.text: Emporium bills itself as Chicago's original arcade bar, and now runs three rooms in the city. The Fulton Market location, at 839 W. Fulton Market, pairs arcade cabinets, pinball and pool tables with a craft beer and cocktail bar, a stage with professional sound and lights, and a 1,500-square-foot patio.
emporium-west-town.descriptor: Arcade bar at 839 W. Fulton Market with pinball, pool and a live-music stage

epic-burger-chicago-loop.text: Epic Burger started in Chicago in 2008 with a pitch it still uses as a tagline — "A More Mindful Burger" — building the chain around non-processed ingredients at an affordable price, eco-friendly packaging and store design. It has since grown to nine Illinois locations.
epic-burger-chicago-loop.descriptor: "A More Mindful Burger" counter on S. State St. near Columbia College

ernest-hemingway-birthplace-museum.text: Ernest Hemingway was born in this Oak Park house on July 21, 1899. The Queen Anne was designed by architect Wesley Arnold and built in 1890 for his grandparents, and was the first home in Oak Park with electricity; the Ernest Hemingway Foundation of Oak Park bought it in 1992, restored it, and opened it to the public as a museum in 2001.
