Rich Melman dreamed up the casual bistro after eating at the fine-dining French room Ambria; steak frites and the roast chicken à la Grand-Mère are still the signatures.
mon-ami-gabi.descriptor: French bistro in the Belden-Stratford, Lincoln Park — steak frites

monadnock-building.text: The Monadnock is really two buildings. Burnham & Root's 1891 north half is the tallest load-bearing masonry building ever erected — brick walls six feet thick at the sidewalk, tapering to 18 inches at the top — while Holabird & Roche's 1893 south half used a steel frame. It also carried America's first portal wind bracing. Finished, it held 1,200 rooms and some 6,000 occupants, the largest office building in the world.
monadnock-building.descriptor: 1891–93 early skyscraper at 53 W. Jackson Blvd. in the Loop

monroe-harbor.text: Monroe Harbor sits at the foot of Monroe Street off Grant Park and holds 824 mooring cans — boats swing on buoys rather than tying up in slips, so the whole fleet floats loose in front of the downtown skyline. It's one of ten harbors in the Chicago Park District system, which at roughly 6,000 boats is the largest municipal harbor network in the country.
monroe-harbor.descriptor: Downtown mooring harbor off Grant Park at the foot of Monroe St

monteverde-restaurant-pastificio.text: Chef Sarah Grueneberg opened Monteverde with partner Meg Sahs in November 2015 and won the James Beard award for Best Chef: Great Lakes in 2017. The pastificio is the whole point — a custom-built pasta lab where cooks make fresh pasta by hand in full view of the dining room. Eater named it one of the 21 best new restaurants in America.
monteverde-restaurant-pastificio.descriptor: Handmade-pasta restaurant at 1020 W. Madison St. in the West Loop

montrose-dog-beach.text: This is one of only two dog beaches in the Chicago Park District — a fenced stretch at the north end of Montrose Beach where dogs run loose on the sand and straight into Lake Michigan. The wider Montrose Beach, in Uptown, is the city's largest.
montrose-dog-beach.descriptor: Fenced off-leash dog beach at the north end of Montrose Beach in Uptown

montrose-harbor.text: The point beside the harbor hides the "Magic Hedge" — honeysuckle planted to camouflage a Cold War Nike missile installation that stood here from 1955 to 1965, and which turned out to be a magnet for migrating birds. With 349 species recorded it is Illinois's hottest eBird spot, and in 2019 the piping plovers Monty and Rose nested on Montrose Beach — Chicago's first since 1948.
montrose-harbor.descriptor: Lakefront harbor and beach at Montrose Ave on the north end of Lincoln Park

monument-of-the-millenium.descriptor: Lakefront monument on the breakwater access beside DuSable Harbor

moody-tongue-brewing-company.text: Brewmaster Jared Rouben runs Moody Tongue as a culinary brewery — chef-driven beers composed like dishes. Alongside the casual taproom bar, its Dining Room serves a ten-plus-course tasting menu paired entirely with beer instead of wine, and is Michelin-starred, a rarity for a brewery.
moody-tongue-brewing-company.descriptor: Chef-driven brewery with a taproom bar and fine-dining beer pairings

moodys-pub.text: Moody's has been charbroiling burgers over an open flame on North Broadway since 1959. The inside is famously dark — beamed ceilings, two roaring fireplaces, candlelit tables and free peanuts, dim enough that Time Out joked you should bring a flashlight to read the menu — and the tree-shaded beer garden out back draws elbow-to-elbow crowds all summer. No reservations.
moodys-pub.descriptor: Edgewater burger-and-beer tavern on N Broadway since 1959

mott-st.text: Chef Edward Kim's Wicker Park dining room serves Asian American plates built for feast-style sharing, drawing on the night markets of Asia and his Korean American childhood — Eastern cooking technique applied to Chicago ingredients.
mott-st.descriptor: Asian American shared-plates restaurant on Ashland Ave in Wicker Park

mr-beef-on-orleans.text: Joe Zucchero opened Mr. Beef in 1979, and the no-frills Orleans Street stand became a Jay Leno favorite and a late-night TV fixture. It is also the inspiration and a filming location for the series The Bear — after the show landed, daily sandwich sales jumped from roughly 300 to more than 800.
mr-beef-on-orleans.descriptor: Italian beef counter on N. Orleans in River North since 1979

muddy-waters.text: This bronze sidewalk plaque is one of the Bronzeville Walk of Fame markers running along Martin Luther King Jr. Drive from 25th to 35th, honoring African-American pioneers. Muddy Waters came north from Mississippi in 1943 and went electric because, as he put it, "couldn't nobody hear you with an acoustic." The Rolling Stones took their name from his 1950 recording "Rollin' Stone."
muddy-waters.descriptor: Bronzeville Walk of Fame plaque on King Drive near 33rd Street

murphys-bleachers.text: There has been a bar on this corner since the 1930s, when Ernie Pareti ran it as Ernie's Bleachers, selling hot dogs and beer by the pail just after Prohibition. As Ray's Bleachers it became headquarters for the Bleacher Bums during the Cubs' 1969 pennant race; former Chicago cop Jim Murphy bought it in 1980, renamed it, and added a rooftop. His daughter Beth has run it since his death in 2003.
murphys-bleachers.descriptor: Wrigleyville sports bar at Sheffield & Waveland behind the Wrigley bleachers

museum-of-contemporary-art.text: Since opening in 1967 the MCA has specialized in firsts: Christo's first wrapped building in America (1969), Frida Kahlo's first U.S. exhibition (1978), and Jeff Koons's first solo museum show (1988). Josef Paul Kleihues designed the current building, opened in 1996 at 220 East Chicago Avenue, which visitors enter by climbing a wide monumental staircase.
museum-of-contemporary-art.descriptor: Contemporary art museum in Streeterville, just off the Magnificent Mile

national-museum-of-mexican-art.text: Founded in 1982 by Carlos Tortolero and a group of Mexican-American teachers, it opened to the public in 1987 and is the only Latino museum accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. Admission is free. Its Día de los Muertos exhibition each October is the largest in the country, and the building's facade borrows from the pre-Columbian friezes at Mitla, Oaxaca.
national-museum-of-mexican-art.descriptor: Free Mexican and Chicano art museum in Pilsen's Harrison Park

navy-pier.text: It opened in 1916 as Municipal Pier, a 3,300-foot dock for freighters and passenger ships. In World War II the Navy turned it into a training center where roughly 18,000 aviators qualified, and the name stuck; from 1946 it served as a University of Illinois campus for returning GIs. Today it draws over nine million visitors a year.
navy-pier.descriptor: 3,300-foot lakefront pier with a 196-foot Ferris wheel, open since 1916

neofuturists.text: Greg Allen founded the Neo-Futurists in 1988 on "an aesthetics of honesty, speed and brevity" — performers play only themselves, on the stage they are actually standing on. Their late-night "Too Much Light Makes the Baby Go Blind" raced through 30 plays in 60 minutes and ran some 28 years before closing on December 31, 2016; its successor, The Infinite Wrench, took over in 2017.
neofuturists.descriptor: The Neo-Futurarium at 5153 N Ashland, home of The Infinite Wrench

nepal-house-near-south-side.text: One of a small family of Chicago Nepali-Indian restaurants — with siblings in Old Town and on Devon Avenue — Nepal House has served the South Loop from 1301 S. Michigan Ave for more than a decade. The Infatuation singles out its not-too-doughy samosas and spicy momo plates as the best things on a long menu that also covers North Indian standards like saag paneer and chicken tikka masala.
nepal-house-near-south-side.descriptor: Nepali-Indian kitchen on S. Michigan Ave in the South Loop, known for momos

next.text: Grant Achatz and Nick Kokonas opened Next in 2011 with a menu that gets scrapped and rebuilt every few months around a new theme — a time period, a place, or tributes to cooks like Julia Child and Charlie Trotter. Seats sell as prepaid tickets rather than reservations, the system Kokonas spun off into Tock, and the place won the James Beard Best New Restaurant award in 2012.
next.descriptor: Ticketed tasting-menu restaurant in Fulton Market that reinvents itself

nickerson-house.text: Banker Samuel M. Nickerson spent $450,000 on this 1883 mansion, whose plain limestone exterior hides interiors so full of marble — 17 kinds of it — that people called the place the "Marble Palace." Edward J. Burling designed it; since 2008 it has been open to the public as the Richard H. Driehaus Museum.
nickerson-house.descriptor: 1883 Gilded Age "Marble Palace" mansion, now the Driehaus Museum

nicks-beer-garden.text: Nick's has been pouring on Milwaukee Avenue near the Damen Blue Line stop since 1977 and bills itself as Chicago's late-night beer garden — open until 4am most nights and 5am on Saturdays, which makes it the last stop once the rest of the strip closes at 2am. The El rumbling past the beer garden every few minutes is part of the deal.
nicks-beer-garden.descriptor: Late-night Wicker Park bar on Milwaukee Ave since 1977

nookies.text: The original Nookies opened on Wells Street in 1973 and spawned a small North Side family: Nookies Too in Lincoln Park in 1982, then Nookies Tree in Lakeview three years later. It's a plain family diner built on pancakes and omelets, still going on Wells Street after 50 years.
nookies.descriptor: Old Town breakfast diner on Wells Street since 1973

noon-o-kabab.text: The Albany Park original of a family Persian restaurant that started out to bring authentic Iranian cooking to Chicagoland, and has since grown to further locations in Highwood, Lincolnwood and Hickory Hills.
noon-o-kabab.descriptor: Persian kabob house on N Kedzie Ave in Albany Park

north-pond.text: The Arts and Crafts building at the edge of Lincoln Park's North Pond went up in 1912 as a warming shelter for ice skaters, later became Park District storage, fell into disrepair, and even ran briefly as a hot dog stand before restaurateur Richard Mott turned it into a restaurant in the late 1990s. It held a Michelin star under chef Bruce Sherman; chef César Murillo now forages his mushrooms and keeps bees and a garden on the roof.
north-pond.descriptor: Seasonal American fine dining in a 1912 Lincoln Park warming house

northerly-island.text: Built in 1925 out of Daniel Burnham's Plan of Chicago, the man-made peninsula hosted the 1933–34 Century of Progress world's fair and then Meigs Field airport. On the night of March 30, 2003, Mayor Richard M. Daley sent crews to gouge X-shaped trenches into the runway, killing the airport overnight; a 40-acre natural area opened on its southern end in 2015, with a concert pavilion to the north.
northerly-island.descriptor: Man-made lakefront peninsula park and concert lawn south of the Loop

nuclear-energy.text: A Henry Moore bronze — part mushroom cloud, part skull — stands on the Ellis Avenue spot where Enrico Fermi's team achieved the world's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, under the west stands of the old Stagg Field, on December 2, 1942. Moore's sculpture was dedicated on the 25th anniversary of that day at 3:36 p.m., the minute the pile went critical.
nuclear-energy.descriptor: Henry Moore bronze on Ellis Ave marking the first nuclear chain reaction

oak-park-conservatory.text: Oak Park residents founded the conservatory as a place to keep the exotic plants they hauled home from their travels; the Edwardian-style glass house standing today was built in 1929. It fell into neglect and was slated for demolition in 1970 until neighbors organized to save it. It now holds more than 3,000 plants — some dating to the original collection — and has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 2005.
oak-park-conservatory.descriptor: 1929 Edwardian glass conservatory on Garfield St, free to visit

obama-family-home.text: Barack and Michelle Obama bought the house at 5046 S. Greenwood Ave. in Kenwood in 2005, putting book-deal proceeds toward the roughly $1.6 million price. It was their home when he was elected president in 2008.
obama-family-home.descriptor: Barack and Michelle Obama's Kenwood house on S. Greenwood Ave.

obama-presidential-center-museum.text: The Obama Presidential Center opened to the public on Juneteenth 2026, on 19 acres of Jackson Park on the South Side. Its 225-foot museum tower — already nicknamed the "Obamalisk" — carries five-foot letters from Obama's 2015 Selma speech. It is the first fully digitized presidential library: the paper records live at a National Archives facility in Hoffman Estates, not on site.
obama-presidential-center-museum.descriptor: Presidential museum in Jackson Park on Chicago's South Side, opened June 2026

offshore-chicago.text: Offshore opened on top of Navy Pier's Festival Hall on May 28, 2019, and at its grand opening that June a Guinness World Records adjudicator measured the deck at 52,310 square feet and certified it the largest rooftop bar in the world. It sits at the far east end of the pier, with the lake on three sides.
offshore-chicago.descriptor: Rooftop bar atop Navy Pier's Festival Hall with Lake Michigan views

old-post-office-site.text: A plaque here, just east of the Lake Street bridge, marks the site of Chicago's first post office. It opened on March 31, 1831 in a log building about where South Water Street met Lake Street near the east end of the bridge, with Jonathan N. Bailey as postmaster; his successor, John S. C. Hogan, moved it to Franklin and South Water in 1832.
old-post-office-site.descriptor: Plaque by the Lake Street bridge marking Chicago's first post office

old-town-ale-house.text: Open since 1958 near Second City, the Ale House is papered with owner Bruce Elliott's paintings — barroom regulars alongside Belushi, Bill Murray and Stephen Colbert, plus satirical portraits of Blagojevich, Palin and Putin. Roger Ebert called it "the best bar in the world that I know about," and his documentary Life Itself was partly filmed here, closing on Elliott's portrait of him.
old-town-ale-house.descriptor: Old Town dive bar on North Avenue since 1958

orange-garden.text: Orange Garden is widely called the oldest Chinese restaurant in Chicago, serving Cantonese-American food in North Center since 1932. Its ten-foot "Chop Suey" neon — which Preservation Chicago called the city's oldest continuously working neon sign — was auctioned off for $17,000 after the family that runs the place found refurbishment, permits and upkeep too costly.
orange-garden.descriptor: Cantonese-American chop suey house on Irving Park Rd since 1932

oriole.text: Noah Sandoval opened Oriole in 2016 and it has held two Michelin stars, sits at #91 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list, and won Sandoval the 2025 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Great Lakes. The contemporary American tasting menu earned four stars from the Chicago Tribune — and there's no dress code.
oriole.descriptor: Two-Michelin-star tasting-menu restaurant on W. Walnut St in the West Loop

our-lady-of-the-angels-school-fire-memor.text: On December 1, 1958, a fire that began in a basement trash barrel at Our Lady of the Angels School killed 92 children and three nuns. Firefighters pulled more than 160 people out. The disaster drove sweeping changes to school fire-safety codes across the country; a monument listing all 95 victims stands at Queen of Heaven Cemetery, and a memorial was reinstalled at the OLA church in 2022.
our-lady-of-the-angels-school-fire-memor.descriptor: Memorial at the site of the 1958 Our Lady of the Angels school fire

writtenFor.name: Our Lady of the Angels School Fire Memorial

owen-bruner-goodman-theatre.text: The Goodman was founded in 1925 as a memorial to Chicago playwright Kenneth Sawyer Goodman, who died in the 1918 flu pandemic, and it's the city's oldest active nonprofit theater. It won the Regional Theatre Tony in 1992, premiered Mamet's American Buffalo and August Wilson's Gem of the Ocean, and moved into its Dearborn Street home in 2000 — where the Owen is one of two auditoriums named for Goodman family donors.
owen-bruner-goodman-theatre.descriptor: Stage inside the Goodman Theatre, 170 N Dearborn in the Loop

oz-park.text: Named in 1976 for L. Frank Baum, who created The Wonderful Wizard of Oz and lived in Chicago's Humboldt Park in the 1890s, this 13-acre park is guarded by four John Kearney sculptures: the Tin Man (1995), made of car bumpers, plus the bronze Cowardly Lion (2001), Scarecrow (2005) and Dorothy with Toto (2007). It also holds the Emerald Garden and Dorothy's Playlot.
oz-park.descriptor: 13-acre Lincoln Park green space with four Wizard of Oz statues

palm-court.text: The lobby lounge of the Drake Hotel has poured afternoon tea for close to a century, for guests including Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana. The three-tiered tray of finger sandwiches, scones and petit fours comes with a choice of 17 teas, and a live harpist plays on select afternoons.
palm-court.descriptor: Afternoon tea lounge in the Drake Hotel lobby, Gold Coast

palmer-square-park.text: Palmer Square is a 7.69-acre link in Chicago's historic boulevard system, laid out in the early 1870s and named for Civil War general and Illinois governor John McAuley Palmer. When the bicycle craze swept Chicago from the mid-1880s on, the oval became a favorite track for "wheelmen," and Schwinn founder Ignaz Schwinn later lived at Palmer and Humboldt. Today a running track rings the green, alongside a playground themed on The Velveteen Rabbit.
palmer-square-park.descriptor: 7.7-acre boulevard park in Logan Square with a loop running track

park-west.text: Opened November 25, 1916 as the Lane Court Theatre, an Ascher Brothers vaudeville and movie house, it showed adult films and live burlesque from the late 1960s before reopening in 1977 as a concert hall holding up to 1,000. Talking Heads' 1982 live album was recorded here, and Elvis Costello, John Prine and Tori Amos all have live recordings or broadcasts from the room.
park-west.descriptor: 1916 vaudeville house turned Lincoln Park concert hall on W Armitage

parlor-pizza-bar.text: The first Parlor, on Green Street in the West Loop. Neapolitan-inspired pies come out of wood-burning ovens topped with fresh local ingredients, sharing the menu with dessert tacos, craft beers and original cocktails, and the expansive patio and rooftop are the summer draw.
parlor-pizza-bar.descriptor: Wood-fired pizza and craft beer at 108 N Green St, with patio and rooftop

writtenFor.name: Parlor Pizza Bar - Fulton Market District

parlor-pizza-bar-fulton-market-district.text: Parlor Pizza Bar has a West Loop room at 108 N. Green St. with patio and rooftop space, plus this Wicker Park location with a patio and an indoor-only spot in River North, pairing pizza with craft beer and cocktails. The same owners run Texan Taco Bar on Randolph Street.
parlor-pizza-bar-fulton-market-district.descriptor: Pizza, craft beer and cocktails with a patio in Wicker Park

parlor-pizza-bar-west-town.text: The newest of the Parlor Pizza Bars, on the corner of Dearborn and Kinzie in River North, serving the same wood-oven Neapolitan-style pies, craft beer and draft cocktails on the patio. Its calling card is a giant J.C. Rivera pizza-wings mural, put there to be photographed.
parlor-pizza-bar-west-town.descriptor: Wood-fired pizza bar at Dearborn and Kinzie in River North

pars-cove-restaurant.text: Owner Max Pars left Iran for Illinois in 1969 to study economics, bought a fried-chicken joint in Albany Park in 1976, and converted it to Persian food because there was, as he put it, no Persian food in Chicago at the time. The Tribune gave the restaurant four-star reviews four years running in the '80s, and his Lincoln Park dining room on West Diversey has been going for decades.
pars-cove-restaurant.descriptor: Persian-Mediterranean kabob house on W Diversey in Lincoln Park

parsons-chicken-fish.text: Parson's is the Logan Square fried-chicken and fish spot from Land and Sea Dept., at 2952 W. Armitage Ave. Its Negroni slushy — the cocktail spun frozen, with Zissou bitters standing in for Campari — is the can't-miss order, and Time Out calls the courtyard one of Chicago's best patios.
parsons-chicken-fish.descriptor: Fried chicken, fish and Negroni slushies with a big Logan Square patio

paulie-gees-logan-square.text: This Paulie Gee's is the Wicker Park slice shop at 1566 N Damen Ave: a New York-style counter turning out 20-inch pies whole or by the slice, including the Hellboy — pepperoni finished with hot honey.
paulie-gees-logan-square.descriptor: NY-style slice shop at 1566 N Damen Ave in Wicker Park, 20-inch pies

pepes-mexican-restaurant.text: Pepe's was started in 1967 by Mario Dovalina and Edwin Ptak and grew from a single neighborhood spot into a Chicago-and-Northwest-Indiana chain of more than 25 restaurants. The locations are individually owned and operated, so the person greeting you at the door is often the owner.
pepes-mexican-restaurant.descriptor: South Side branch of Pepe's, the Chicago Mexican chain founded in 1967

pequods-pizzeria.text: Burt Katz opened the first Pequod's in Morton Grove in 1971 and sold it in 1985; the Clybourn Avenue location carries on his signature move — mozzarella packed against the pan's rim so it bakes into a dark, crunchy ring of caramelized cheese around the pie. Katz had worked the technique out years earlier at The Inferno in Evanston, and later took it to Burt's Place.
pequods-pizzeria.descriptor: Deep-dish with a caramelized cheese crust on Clybourn in Lincoln Park

petterinos.text: Petterino's has been an old-school Italian-American room in the heart of Chicago's Loop and Theatre District for 25 years, and it plays the part: red leather booths and walls lined with caricatures of the politicians, celebrities and influential Chicagoans who have eaten there.
petterinos.descriptor: Old-school Italian-American restaurant in Chicago's Loop theater district

pho-777.text: Phở 777 sits on the Argyle Street strip in Uptown, where The Infatuation calls its phở one of the best bowls in the city — sweet but balanced with beef and warming spices. The big dining room supplies its own entertainment, with TVs going and a light projecting images of the dishes across the space.
pho-777.descriptor: Vietnamese phở and bánh cuốn house on the Argyle strip in Uptown

pho-xe-tang-tank-noodle.text: A cornerstone of Uptown's Vietnamese restaurant strip, Tank Noodle is run by the Ly family and has been voted the city's best Vietnamese restaurant by the Chicago Reader three times. The long menu runs from pho and vermicelli to catfish claypot dishes and the Sriracha fries invented for its Lollapalooza stand.
pho-xe-tang-tank-noodle.descriptor: Family-run Vietnamese pho house in Uptown

phoenix.text: The Chinatown Chamber of Commerce holds its annual Lunar New Year Dinner at Phoenix.
phoenix.descriptor: Chinese restaurant on Archer Ave in Chinatown (萬濠酒家)

phyllis-musical-inn.text: Accordionist Phyllis Jaskot opened this corner bar at Division and Wood as a polka club in 1954, in the "Polish Broadway" era when novelist Nelson Algren prowled the neighborhood — which makes it Wicker Park's oldest live music venue. The Jaskot family still runs it, the glass-block exterior has barely changed, and the bands now lean garage and alternative rather than polka.
phyllis-musical-inn.descriptor: Wicker Park dive bar with a beer garden and near-nightly live bands

piccolo-sogno.text: Chef Tony Priolo, formerly of Coco Pazzo, and wine specialist Ciro Longobardo opened Piccolo Sogno — "little dream" in Italian — at Halsted and Grand on July 16, 2008. The kitchen runs on handmade pasta, wood-fired cooking and an all-Italian wine list, and there is a garden patio set back from the street.
piccolo-sogno.descriptor: Rustic Italian with a garden patio at Halsted & Grand, open since 2008

piece-brewery-pizzeria.text: Bill Jacobs moved to Chicago in 1983 and couldn't find the New Haven thin crust he grew up on, so he recruited high school friend Ray Peck — who had roots at Sally's Apizza in New Haven — and converted a classic bowstring-truss roofing and construction building in Wicker Park into Piece, which opened in July 2001. The brewery has since taken 29 medals, its Golden Arm winning bronze at both the Great American Beer Festival and the World Beer Cup, and Cheap Trick's Rick Nielsen is a co-owner.
piece-brewery-pizzeria.descriptor: New Haven-style thin-crust pizza and brewpub on North Ave, Wicker Park

pier-park.text: Navy Pier opened to the public on July 15, 1916, and Pier Park's Centennial Wheel arrived for the pier's 100th birthday in 2016 — 196 feet tall, 46 feet taller than the wheel it replaced. The original 1995 Ferris wheel wasn't scrapped: it was retired on September 27, 2015, and moved to Branson, Missouri, where it reopened in 2016. A ride now runs three revolutions over twelve minutes instead of seven.
pier-park.descriptor: Navy Pier's amusement area, home of the 196-foot Centennial Wheel

pioneer-zephyr.text: On May 26, 1934 this Burlington streamliner ran Denver to Chicago nonstop — 1,015 miles in 13 hours 5 minutes, averaging 77 mph and touching 112.5 mph — arriving on the opening day of the Century of Progress world's fair. The dash inspired the 1934 film "The Silver Streak," which borrowed the train's nickname. Retired in 1960, it was donated to the museum on the 26th anniversary of the run, to the day.
pioneer-zephyr.descriptor: 1934 stainless-steel streamliner train at the Museum of Science and Industry

pizanos-pizza.text: Pizano's was opened in 1991 by Rudy Malnati Jr.; the family says his father, Rudy Malnati Sr., established Pizzeria Uno in 1943 and introduced Chicago's original deep dish. The Loop shop at 61 E. Madison runs on those family recipes and has been name-checked everywhere from Oprah to the Today show.
pizanos-pizza.descriptor: Deep-dish and thin-crust pizzeria at 61 E. Madison in the Loop

pizanos-pizza-pasta.text: This is the South Loop outpost of Pizano's, opened in 1991 by Rudy Malnati Jr.; the family says his father, Rudy Malnati Sr., established Pizzeria Uno in 1943 and introduced Chicago's original deep dish. Same family recipes, deep dish and pasta, a few blocks from the Prairie Avenue district.
pizanos-pizza-pasta.descriptor: Deep-dish pizza and pasta on S. Indiana Ave in the South Loop

pizzeria-due.text: Ike Sewell, who founded Pizzeria Uno with Ric Riccardo in 1943, opened Due one block away in 1955; the names are simply Italian for one and two. Uno's claim to have invented Chicago deep dish is contested, though: a 1956 Chicago Daily News article credited cook Rudy Malnati Sr. with the original recipe.
pizzeria-due.descriptor: Deep-dish pizzeria in River North, Pizzeria Uno's sibling since 1955

pizzeria-uno.text: Ike Sewell and Ric Riccardo opened Pizzeria Uno in 1943, and it is generally credited with inventing Chicago deep-dish pizza. Credit is contested even inside its own kitchen: original pizza chef Rudy Malnati — father of Lou Malnati — has also been named as the recipe's creator, and cook Alice Mae Redmond later reworked the dough with water and olive oil.
pizzeria-uno.descriptor: Near North Side deep-dish pizzeria, open since 1943

polk-bros-park.text: Navy Pier's 13-acre front lawn, opened in 2016 after the Polk family — whose foundation was started by appliance retailer Sol Polk — gave $20 million to the pier's redevelopment. The centerpiece fountain is a summer splash pad that freezes into a lighted ice rink in winter, and its City and Lake stages help carry the more than 245 free public programs Navy Pier offers each year.
polk-bros-park.descriptor: Navy Pier's 13-acre front lawn; fountain doubles as a winter ice rink

pompei.text: Luigi Davino opened Pompei as a bakery in 1909, with the family living above the shop and selling only bread and cheese pizza, and named it for the nearby Our Lady of Pompeii church. It has served families for five generations — Luigi's eldest son Alphonso ran the bakery for three decades after World War II, and when he retired in the 1980s his nephew Ralph took over.
pompei.descriptor: Family-run Little Italy bakery and pizzeria on Taylor St since 1909

pops-for-champagne.text: A champagne bar that spent years in Lakeview before moving to River North at the end of 2006. Alongside the sparkling-wine list it works as a jazz room, booking high-quality mainstream jazz from accomplished Chicago-area pianists and vocalists; the same operators run a sister bar, Watershed.
pops-for-champagne.descriptor: Champagne bar and jazz room at State and Ohio in River North

portage-park.text: The park takes its name from the old portage route used by Native people and fur traders along what is now Irving Park Road. Its pool was rebuilt to Olympic size in 1959 for the Pan American Games, and in 1972 Portage Park hosted the U.S. Olympic swimming trials, where Mark Spitz set world records. The 36-acre grounds, on the National Register since 1995, include a Clarence Hatzfeld fieldhouse.
portage-park.descriptor: 36-acre Northwest Side park with an Olympic-sized pool, opened 1913

prairie-avenue-historic-district.text: From the 1870s to the 1890s this was Chicago's richest street — Marshall Field, George Pullman and Philip Armour all built here, and an 1893 guidebook called it the most expensive street west of Fifth Avenue. H.H. Richardson's fortress-like Glessner House (1886) survived a 1960s teardown fight and is now a museum. The street's north end is also the site of the 1812 Battle of Fort Dearborn.
prairie-avenue-historic-district.descriptor: Gilded Age mansion row on the Near South Side, anchored by Glessner House

prime-provisions.text: A LaSalle Street steakhouse styled after early-20th-century supper clubs, with a 500-square-foot dry-aging room lined with Himalayan rock salt. Steaks are hand-cut, fired in a 1,200-degree broiler and sent out on heated plates with sea salt and Wisconsin grass-fed butter.
prime-provisions.descriptor: Loop steakhouse on N. LaSalle with a Himalayan-salt dry-aging room

pritzker-family-childrens-zoo.text: Opened in 2004 inside Lincoln Park Zoo — one of the few free zoos in the country, running since 1868 — the children's zoo sticks to North American natives: black bears, red wolves, river otters, beavers and native turtles. Outside are the Wild Sapling Play Forest, with a log tower and vine tunnel, and a wheelchair-accessible play treehouse.
pritzker-family-childrens-zoo.descriptor: Children's zoo at free-admission Lincoln Park Zoo, opened 2004

pui-tak-center.text: Completed in 1927 and opened in 1928 as the On Leong Merchants Association Building — a terra-cotta Western take on Chinese architecture — it served as Chinatown's immigrant aid center and unofficial "city hall." A 1988 FBI raid turned up a hidden second-floor casino and the government seized the building; the Chinese Christian Union Church bought it in 1993 and reopened it as the Pui Tak Center. It's a Chicago Landmark.
pui-tak-center.descriptor: 1928 On Leong Building, Chinatown's landmark at 2216 S Wentworth

qing-xiang-yuan-dumplings.text: A dumpling specialist tucked into the Richland Center mall at 2002 S Wentworth in Chinatown, turning out dumplings across a long list of fillings — lamb and coriander, pork and zucchini, shrimp and leek. Local critics single out the lamb-and-coriander ones, "bursting with juicy, well-seasoned meat."
qing-xiang-yuan-dumplings.descriptor: Chinatown dumpling house in Richland Center on S Wentworth Ave

quartino-ristorante.text: Quartino opened on State Street in 2005 as Gibsons Restaurant Group's Italian shared-plates room: DOP salumi and cheeses sliced from a vintage salumeria case, pasta hand-cut in its own pasta kitchen, and pizza fired in a display hearth oven, backed by a wine list built on small family-owned Italian estates.
quartino-ristorante.descriptor: Italian small plates and wine bar on N State St, River North, since 2005

rainbo-club.text: A Polish polka lounge for decades — owner Dee Taira, who bought it in 1985 from Rose Podulka, cites 1935 as the bar's opening year — the Rainbo became Wicker Park's artist and indie-rock clubhouse. Liz Phair says the cover of "Exile in Guyville" was shot in its photo booth, and Nelson Algren is believed to have drunk here and modeled the Tug & Maul in "The Man with the Golden Arm" on it.
rainbo-club.descriptor: Cash-only Wicker Park dive bar on Damen Ave. with a photo booth

ramen-san.text: Lettuce Entertain You carved this noodle bar out of its Paris Club space on Hubbard Street in 2014, and it still pitches itself as a joint for "hot broth, ice-cold beer and the best '90s hip-hop in town." The 10 Hour Tonkotsu is the house bowl; late-night fried rice with chashu burnt ends is the closer.
ramen-san.descriptor: Ramen bar on Hubbard St in River North; 10-hour tonkotsu, '90s hip-hop

ramen-san-lincoln-park.text: Ramen-San is Lettuce Entertain You's noodle bar, which bills itself as a neighborhood joint slinging "hot broth, ice-cold beer and the best '90s hip-hop in town." The Lincoln Park room is one of four Chicago outposts, alongside River North, the Fulton Market whisky bar and the Streeterville "Deluxe" with its own sushi and maki program.
ramen-san-lincoln-park.descriptor: Lettuce Entertain You ramen shop at 1962 N Halsted, '90s hip-hop on the stereo

ramen-san-river-north.text: Lettuce Entertain You's Ramen-San calls itself a neighborhood noodle joint slinging hot broth, ice-cold beer and the best '90s hip-hop in town. The Streeterville outpost is the "Deluxe" version at 165 E. Huron; the house bowl is the 10 Hour Tonkotsu — rich pork broth with pork belly, a molten egg, bamboo and wakame over Tokyo wavy noodles.
ramen-san-river-north.descriptor: Ramen-San Deluxe at 165 E Huron in Streeterville: tonkotsu and sake bombs

ramen-san-streeterville.text: The Fulton Market branch of Ramen-San, Lettuce Entertain You's noodle-shop concept built around hot broth, ice-cold beer and '90s hip-hop. It's the one location, at 219 N. Green Street, that pairs the ramen counter with a whisky bar.
ramen-san-streeterville.descriptor: Lettuce Entertain You ramen bar on N Green St with a whisky bar

ramova-theatre.text: Built in 1929 by Lithuanian businessman Jokubas Maskoliunas, the 1,300-seat Ramova was an "atmospheric" theater, with false fronts and balconies rigged to look like a Spanish courtyard. It sat dark for years until Tyler Nevius bought it from the city for $1 in 2017 and rebuilt it with 55 investors including Quincy Jones, Jennifer Hudson and Chance the Rapper; it reopened New Year's Eve 2023.
ramova-theatre.descriptor: 1929 atmospheric movie palace on S Halsted in Bridgeport, now a music venue

ranallis-west-loop.text: Ranalli's took over the old WestEnd Bar & Grill space on Madison Street in 2021, opened by Four Corners Tavern Group with a redesign by Studio K and Chicago artist Anthony Lewellen. The Ranalli's pizza name goes back to a Lincoln Park original that opened about 45 years earlier, in the mid-1970s.
ranallis-west-loop.descriptor: Pizza and game-day bar at 1326 W. Madison St. in the West Loop

rate-field.text: Opened in 1991 as Comiskey Park II, it was the first major sports facility built in Chicago since 1929 and the last big-league park finished before the retro-ballpark wave of the 1990s. It has carried four names since, through U.S. Cellular Field and Guaranteed Rate Field to plain Rate Field in 2024, and it kept one old tradition: an updated version of Bill Veeck's exploding scoreboard from 1960.
rate-field.descriptor: White Sox ballpark on W 35th Street in Armour Square, opened 1991

redhot-ranch.text: A no-frills, cash-only stand doing Depression-style dogs — yellow mustard, onions, sport peppers and a handful of fries piled right into the bun — for around five bucks with fries, plus burgers. Unusually for a Chicago dog stand, it has roomy indoor seating and a real bathroom.
redhot-ranch.descriptor: Cash-only Depression-style hot dog stand on W Armitage

redhot-ranch-lake-view.text: The roomier sibling of the Armitage original — TVs, actual seats, and the same Depression-style dogs. Thin griddled cheeseburgers with melted cheese, LTO and special sauce, plus fried shrimp with spicy cocktail sauce, round out a menu built for after last call.
redhot-ranch-lake-view.descriptor: Late-night hot dog, burger and fried shrimp stand on N Ashland in Lake View

replay-andersonville.text: Replay is an arcade bar on the Northalsted strip: the classic cabinets are free to play, with premium games like pinball and Mario Kart on coin, plus bourbon, a back patio and free popcorn. It belongs to the same local hospitality group as Hydrate nightclub, Elixir and the Andersonville Replay.
replay-andersonville.descriptor: Arcade bar on North Halsted with pinball, patio and free popcorn

revolution-brewing-kedzie-brewery.text: Josh Deth started Revolution in 2010 with a Logan Square brewpub and opened this Kedzie Avenue production brewery in spring 2012, about a mile away. At 90,000 square feet it is the largest independently owned brewery in Illinois, home of Anti-Hero IPA, with a German beer-hall-style taproom pouring 20 drafts plus Saturday public brewery tours.
revolution-brewing-kedzie-brewery.descriptor: Revolution's 90,000 sq ft Avondale brewery with a beer-hall taproom on Kedzie

rice-amplitheater-abbott-oceanarium.text: Opened in 1991 and known since 2010 as the Abbott Oceanarium, it is the largest indoor marine mammal facility in the world — 3 million gallons of water in total, including the 2-million-gallon "Whale Harbour," home to beluga whales and Pacific white-sided dolphins beside Lake Michigan. A 1,000-seat amphitheater inside presents the marine mammal show.
rice-amplitheater-abbott-oceanarium.descriptor: Shedd Aquarium's lakefront Oceanarium wing and marine-mammal amphitheater

richard-h-driehaus-museum.text: Banker Samuel Nickerson took four years to build this 1883 house, reportedly the most expensive and elaborate private residence in Chicago when it was finished; 17 kinds of marble plus onyx and alabaster earned it the nickname the "Marble Palace." Richard Driehaus bought it in 2003 and opened it as a museum in 2008 — Gilded Age rooms hung with Tiffany glass and European decorative arts.
richard-h-driehaus-museum.descriptor: Gilded Age museum in the 1883 Nickerson mansion on E Erie St

richards-bar.text: A dark but tidy River West dive that borrows a few traditions from across the Atlantic: the bartender works in a crisp white button-down, hard-boiled eggs go for 75 cents, and outsized Robert De Niro posters watch the room over $3.50 beers.
richards-bar.descriptor: Old-school dive bar on W Grand Ave in River West

ricobenes.text: Ricobene's has been going since 1946 and is known citywide for the breaded steak sandwich: a cutlet fried crisp, bathed in chunky bright-red tomato sauce and stuffed into a roll with cheese that turns melty within seconds. It's a Chicago late-night staple on W. 26th St., open until 2 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
ricobenes.descriptor: Late-night spot on W. 26th St. known for the breaded steak sandwich, since 1946

river-shannon.text: A Lincoln Park Irish pub going on six decades, with an antique wooden bar, about a dozen Irish whiskeys, theme nights, and photographs of the early-1900s South Side on the walls.
river-shannon.descriptor: Irish neighborhood pub on W Armitage in Lincoln Park

riviera-theatre.text: Rapp and Rapp built the Riviera in 1917 as a movie palace for the Balaban & Katz chain, and in the Jazz Age it paired films with live jazz. In the 1980s the main-floor seats came out and it became a standing concert room; Jam Productions has owned it since 2006, at about 2,500 capacity.
riviera-theatre.descriptor: 1917 Uptown movie palace turned 2,500-capacity rock venue

rj-grunts.text: R.J. Grunts opened June 10, 1971, the first restaurant from Rich Melman and Jerry Orzoff, whose Lettuce Entertain You group has since grown past 100 restaurants. Steps from Lincoln Park Zoo, it still runs on '70s decor, burgers, a build-your-own salad bar and hand-spun malts and shakes; its chili was named Chicago's best in 1979.
rj-grunts.descriptor: 1971 burgers-and-salad-bar joint by Lincoln Park Zoo, LEYE's first

rj-grunts-burger-and-fries.text: The R.J. Grunts name goes back to 1971, when it opened in Lincoln Park as the very first Lettuce Entertain You restaurant. Its salad bar, with more than 50 ingredients daily right down to the pudding, was dubbed one of the first in the country, and burgers, barbecue baby back ribs and hand-dipped malts are still the calling cards.
rj-grunts-burger-and-fries.descriptor: Burgers, fries and hand-dipped malts counter on the Midway Airport grounds

roberts-temple-church-of-god-in-christ.text: On September 3, 1955, about 2,000 mourners packed this church and thousands more waited outside for Emmett Till's funeral, which his mother Mamie Till-Mobley insisted be open-casket: "I just wanted the world to see." Chicago landmarked the building in 2005, and in 2023 it became part of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument.
roberts-temple-church-of-god-in-christ.descriptor: 1922 Bronzeville church on S State St, site of Emmett Till's 1955 funeral

writtenFor.name: Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ

robinsons.descriptor: Barbecue counter in the lower-level food court at 222 S. Riverside Plaza

ron-of-japan.text: A Streeterville teppanyaki room in the Benihana mold: chefs cook filet mignon, lobster tail, chicken or tofu on a sizzling iron plate set into each table, so dinner doubles as a table-side performance. The shrimp kogane-yaki starter arrives under an egg-yolk sauce.
ron-of-japan.descriptor: Teppanyaki steakhouse on E Ontario St in Streeterville, cooked tableside

roof-on-thewit.text: ROOF sits 27 stories up on theWit at 201 N. State Street in the Loop. A retractable roof and climate-controlled space let it open to the skyline in summer and keep running through Chicago winters.
roof-on-thewit.descriptor: 27th-floor rooftop bar atop theWit hotel at State and Lake

rosas-lounge.text: Tony Mangiullo left Italy and landed in Chicago on August 15, 1978; his first night out took him to Theresa's Lounge, where he met Junior Wells. In 1984 he opened this Armitage Avenue club and named it for his mother, Rosa, who followed him over and helped him run it. Honeyboy Edwards, Pinetop Perkins, Billy Branch and Lurrie Bell have all played the room.
rosas-lounge.descriptor: Family-run blues club on W Armitage in Logan Square since 1984

roscoes-tavern-cafe.text: A Halsted Street mainstay since 1987, Roscoe's runs several bars, a dance floor and an outdoor patio, with drag shows, karaoke, dueling pianos and packed RuPaul's Drag Race viewing parties. Eater Chicago named it one of the city's essential LGBTQ bars in 2018 — the same year Mick Jagger turned up to watch two Drag Race queens perform.
roscoes-tavern-cafe.descriptor: Gay bar with dance floor and patio on N Halsted, open since 1987

rose-mary.text: Top Chef winner Joe Flamm crosses his Italian cooking with Croatian food here, handmade pastas and grilled fish alongside cevapi, in what he calls "Adriatic drinking food." The name honors his two grandmothers, Mary and Mary Rose, plus the rosemary that grows along the Italian and Croatian coasts, and the room is styled after a Croatian konoba tavern.
rose-mary.descriptor: Croatian-Italian "Adriatic drinking food" in Fulton Market from Joe Flamm

rosenwald-courts.text: Julius Rosenwald, then head of Sears, Roebuck, built these 421 apartments around a large landscaped courtyard in 1929 as privately funded housing for Black residents of Bronzeville, modeled on Harlem's Dunbar Apartments. Gwendolyn Brooks, Nat King Cole, Joe Louis and Quincy Jones all lived here. Emptied in 2000 and left to decay, it reopened in 2016 after a $109 million restoration as mixed-income housing.
rosenwald-courts.descriptor: 1929 Bronzeville garden-apartment complex built by Sears' Julius Rosenwald

rpm-italian.text: RPM Italian opened in February 2012 on Illinois Street in River North, a partnership between Lettuce Entertain You's Melman siblings — RJ, Jerrod and Molly — and Bill and Giuliana Rancic; Bill won the first season of The Apprentice. The kitchen makes its pasta in house, and the bucatini on the menu is named for Giuliana's mother.
rpm-italian.descriptor: River North Italian from the Melmans and the Rancics, 52 W Illinois

russian-tea-time.text: Ukrainian American Vadim Muchnik and his mother Klara, from Tashkent, opened it in September 1993 as the Russian Tea Room, changing the name after a trademark violation. The Loop room serves afternoon tea, caviar, house-infused vodka and dishes from across Eastern Europe and Central Asia; after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine it drew online vitriol despite never being Russian-owned.
russian-tea-time.descriptor: Eastern European and Central Asian dining room at 77 E. Adams St. since 1993

sabri-nihari.text: The house is named for its signature dish: nihari, which Time Out calls a spicy Pakistani pot roast, served under a slick of ghee that you stir into the gingery gravy before spooning it over rice. It sits at 2502 W Devon Ave, on the South Asian restaurant stretch of Devon Avenue in West Ridge.
sabri-nihari.descriptor: Pakistani restaurant on Devon Ave in West Ridge, named for its nihari stew

saigon-sisters.text: Sisters Mary Nguyen Aregoni and Theresa Nguyen started Saigon Sisters in 2009 as a stall in the Chicago French Market, where their mother, Mama Suu, worked the pho station serving banh mi, spring rolls, pho and bao. The family, whose food business roots run back to Laos, immigrated to the U.S. in 1976; the West Loop restaurant on Lake Street followed.
saigon-sisters.descriptor: Vietnamese-French cafe on W. Lake St. — banh mi, pho, spring rolls

saint-valentines-day-massacre.text: On February 14, 1929, seven men from Bugs Moran's North Side Gang were lined up against the back wall of a garage here and shot with Thompson submachine guns by killers, two of them dressed as police. The murders were pinned on Al Capone's Outfit, though Capone was in Florida at the time. The garage was torn down in 1967 and the site is now a lawn; bricks from the wall ended up in a Las Vegas museum.
saint-valentines-day-massacre.descriptor: Site of the 1929 gangland massacre at 2122 N. Clark St, Lincoln Park

san-soo-gab-san.text: A Lincoln Square Korean barbecue that grills over real charcoal, which Time Out warns leaves you with "the essence of ash" in your clothes. The wang kalbi and dai ji kalbi are marinated rather than drowned, and there is cold bibim naeng myun for anyone dodging the smoke. Michelin gave it a Bib Gourmand in 2011.
san-soo-gab-san.descriptor: Charcoal Korean barbecue on N Western Ave in Lincoln Square, open late

sawada-coffee.text: Founded by champion Japanese latte artist Hiroshi Sawada, who runs five shops in Japan, as his first stateside location — on a raised platform at the back of Green Street Smoked Meats. The signature Military Latte pairs double espresso with matcha and vanilla syrup under latte art in a martial insignia.
sawada-coffee.descriptor: West Loop coffee bar behind Green Street Smoked Meats; Military Latte

schubas-tavern.text: The building is one of the tied houses the Schlitz brewery put up around Chicago from the late 1880s — saloons it owned outright so its beer was the only beer on tap — most of them stamped with the company's logo in a concrete relief in the brickwork. Mike and Chris Schuba ran it as a music room for two decades before opening Lincoln Hall in 2009.
schubas-tavern.descriptor: Live-music tavern in a former Schlitz tied house at Belmont and Southport

schwa.text: Michael Carlson opened Schwa in 2005 in an 825-square-foot Ashland Avenue storefront: 26 seats, no waitstaff — the cooks plate and serve — and no liquor license, so guests bring their own bottles. It holds a Michelin star, fields around 60 reservation requests a day for those 26 seats, and its signature course is a quail egg ravioli.
schwa.descriptor: 26-seat BYOB tasting-menu counter on N Ashland in Wicker Park

scofflaw.text: Named for the word coined in a 1923 Boston Herald contest for people who flouted Prohibition, Scofflaw took over the Streetside Cafe space in Logan Square and opened in 2012 as a gin-focused cocktail bar. The Victorian-style salon still turns out small plates well beyond bar food, and fresh-baked cookies at midnight.
scofflaw.descriptor: Gin-focused cocktail bar at 3201 W Armitage Ave in Logan Square

sepia.text: Sepia opened in 2007 in a former 1890s print shop on Jefferson Street, keeping the old wood and exposed brick and adding a custom Art Nouveau tile floor. It has held a Michelin star every year since 2011, and Andrew Zimmerman ran the kitchen for 16 years before handing off to Kyle Cottle at the end of 2025.
sepia.descriptor: Michelin-starred contemporary American in an 1890s West Loop print shop

shanghai-terrace.text: The Peninsula Chicago's Cantonese-Shanghainese restaurant sits on the hotel's fourth floor just off Michigan Avenue, with a terrace decked in fresh flowers and views of the historic Water Tower — a rare quiet perch above the Mag Mile. The kitchen runs dim sum alongside plates like five-spiced duck and wok-baked lobster.
shanghai-terrace.descriptor: Cantonese-Shanghainese dining on The Peninsula's fourth-floor terrace

shaws-crab-house.text: Shaw's opened on Hubbard Street in 1984 and has kept a 1940s-style setting ever since, split between a white-tablecloth main dining room and a louder oyster bar with live blues on Thursdays. It's a Lettuce Entertain You restaurant and flies its catch in coast-to-coast, working directly with fishermen and farmers.
shaws-crab-house.descriptor: 1940s-style seafood house and oyster bar on E Hubbard since 1984

shedd-aquarium.text: Retail executive John G. Shedd gave the city the aquarium, which opened in 1930 after his death. To fill the saltwater tanks a thousand miles inland, twenty railroad tank cars made eight round trips to Key West that year hauling a million gallons of seawater, making Shedd the first inland aquarium with a permanent saltwater collection.
shedd-aquarium.descriptor: Lakefront aquarium on the Museum Campus, opened 1930

sheffields.text: Just south of Wrigley Field at Sheffield and School, Sheffield's has been pouring for more than 30 years and says it pioneered Chicago's craft-beer movement — four bars, two fireplaces, 100-plus bottles and a vintage beer list. It smokes its own brisket and baby back ribs in a hickory smoker, and Food & Wine has named its garden one of America's best beer gardens.
sheffields.descriptor: Craft-beer bar and BBQ smokehouse with a beer garden south of Wrigley

shoreline-sightseeing.text: Shoreline started in 1939, when Jim Martin ran twenty-five-cent speedboat rides off the Shedd Aquarium, and it has stayed in the same family ever since — his brother George, then George's nephew Charles Collopy, then Collopy's sons. The red-white-and-blue color scheme dates to a 1960 boat, the Marlyn, and the architecture river tour that now defines the company only launched in 1999.
shoreline-sightseeing.descriptor: Chicago boat tour operator running architecture cruises and water taxis since 1939

sidetrack.text: Art Johnston and Jose 'Pepe' Peña opened Sidetrack in 1982. It has since spread across eight storefronts into a 15,000-square-foot, six-room bar with a rooftop deck, built around its themed video nights, and the Sun-Times has called it one of the world's top gay bars. It has also used its size politically, boycotting Stoli in 2013 over Russia's anti-gay laws.
sidetrack.descriptor: Video bar on N. Halsted in Northalsted, open since 1982

siena-tavern.text: Top Chef alum Fabio Viviani leads the kitchen at this River North Italian room from the DineAmic hospitality group, turning out made-from-scratch pasta and thin-crust pizzas, with a crudo bar up front. It draws a crowd — Time Out arrived at 6pm on a Tuesday and found the place full.
siena-tavern.descriptor: Fabio Viviani's Italian restaurant at 51 W. Kinzie St. in River North

simons-tavern.text: A holdout from Andersonville's Swedish era, Simon's is a former basement speakeasy on Clark Street whose interior was modeled on the S.S. Normandie, the largest ocean liner of the 1930s. It still pours glögg, the Scandinavian mulled wine, when the weather turns.
simons-tavern.descriptor: Swedish-rooted Andersonville dive on Clark St, known for seasonal glögg

site-of-fort-dearborn.text: Fort Dearborn, a log stockade built in 1803, stood here at the mouth of the Chicago River. On August 15, 1812 its garrison and settlers evacuated and were ambushed nearby — 86 of the 148 who left were killed — and the fort was burned. Rebuilt in 1816, decommissioned by 1837 and finished off by the 1871 fire, its footprint is now traced by bronze markers in the sidewalk.
site-of-fort-dearborn.descriptor: Marked site of the 1803 U.S. Army fort at Michigan Ave and Wacker Dr

skydeck-chicago-willis-tower.text: The Skydeck opened in 1974 on the 103rd floor of what was then the Sears Tower, 1,353 feet up. In 2009 it added The Ledge, all-glass balconies that cantilever about four feet out from the facade, floor included, so you can stand out over Wacker Drive on three layers of laminated glass. There are five of them today, the newest added in 2022.
skydeck-chicago-willis-tower.descriptor: 103rd-floor observation deck in Willis Tower with the glass Ledge boxes

sluggers-world-class-sports-bar.text: Steve Strauss opened Sluggers in a former auto body garage on Clark Street in 1985, a couple of blocks from Wrigley Field. The second floor is the real draw — the indoor batting cages the bar built its name on, plus dueling pianos, above the 40-odd TVs downstairs.
sluggers-world-class-sports-bar.descriptor: Wrigleyville sports bar with upstairs batting cages, open since 1985

small-cheval.text: Small Cheval is the stripped-down offshoot of Au Cheval, Brendan Sodikoff's diner known for its cheeseburger. The first one opened in 2015 with a slightly smaller, cheaper version of that burger — thin patties, Dijon, onion, pickles — plus fries and shakes, and it has since grown into a handful of locations under the Hogsalt group.
small-cheval.descriptor: Au Cheval's burger-only spinoff — double cheeseburger, fries and shakes

small-cheval-lake-view-east.text: Small Cheval is the pared-down burger counter from Hogsalt, the Chicago restaurant group that also runs Au Cheval. The menu is short — cheeseburgers with griddled onions and melted cheese, fries, milkshakes and cocktails — and the Old Town shop sits at 1345 N. Wells St.
small-cheval-lake-view-east.descriptor: Counter-service burger shop at 1345 N. Wells St. in Old Town

small-cheval-west-town.text: Small Cheval is Brendan Sodikoff's pared-down offshoot of Au Cheval, built around a version of that restaurant's famous cheeseburger: super-thin griddled patties, melted cheese, Dijon, onion and pickles, served slightly smaller and a little cheaper. The first one opened in Wicker Park; it has since grown into a handful of locations under his Hogsalt group.
small-cheval-west-town.descriptor: Au Cheval's burger spinoff — griddled double cheeseburgers and fries

smart-bar.text: Joe Shanahan opened smartbar in July 1982 in a building put up in 1927 as a Swedish community center; he then took over the main-floor hall upstairs, booking R.E.M. for one of its first shows as the rock club Metro. The club still runs out of the century-old basement auditorium at 3730 N Clark, where it has programmed dance music for four decades.
smart-bar.descriptor: Basement dance club under Metro at 3730 N Clark, open since 1982

smoque-bbq.text: Five friends opened Smoque at 3800 N Pulaski in Old Irving Park in late 2006. They make their rubs, sauces and sides from scratch and match each cut of meat to its own rub, wood smoke, sauce and cooking technique, arguing barbecue is best when all those flavors harmonize.
smoque-bbq.descriptor: Old Irving Park barbecue counter on N Pulaski, house-made rubs, since 2006

smyth.text: Smyth opened in 2016 on the second floor above The Loyalist, the bar its owners run downstairs. Chef John Shields' seasonal tasting menu has earned three Michelin stars — currently the only three-star restaurant in Chicago.
smyth.descriptor: Three-Michelin-star tasting menu above The Loyalist, West Loop

soldier-field.text: Opened in 1924 as Grant Park Stadium and renamed a year later for American soldiers who died in World War I, it has been the Bears' home since 1971. A 2003 rebuild dropped a modern bowl inside the original neoclassical colonnades, a move jarring enough that the federal government stripped the stadium of its National Historic Landmark status in 2006.
soldier-field.descriptor: Lakefront NFL stadium with Doric colonnades, home of the Chicago Bears

southport-grocery-cafe.text: A from-scratch breakfast-and-lunch cafe and specialty grocery at 3552 N Southport in Lakeview, known for its specialty pancakes and cupcakes. The shelves stock its own preserves, pickles and mustards, and the Southport Cuban is built on house-smoked brisket with ham, gruyère, dijonnaise, giardiniera and arugula.
southport-grocery-cafe.descriptor: Lakeview cafe and pantry shop on Southport Ave, known for pancakes and cupcakes

spacca-napoli.text: Jonathan Goldsmith is a certified pizzaiuolo who oversees the dough and the pizza-making himself, and his oven was built by artisans from Naples. Spacca Napoli has been baking to strict Neapolitan spec on Sunnyside Avenue in Ravenswood for close to 20 years, and doubles as an art space for Goldsmith's partner, artist Ginny Sykes, whose studio is upstairs.
spacca-napoli.descriptor: Neapolitan pizzeria on W. Sunnyside Ave. in Ravenswood, Naples-built oven

spinning-j.text: A bakery and old-style soda fountain at 1000 N. California Ave. in Humboldt Park, pouring shakes, sodas and floats alongside the pies it is best known for — the Thanksgiving lineup has run to cranberry yuzu meringue, s'mores and Key lime hibiscus. It marked its tenth anniversary in 2025.
spinning-j.descriptor: Humboldt Park bakery and soda fountain on California Ave, known for pies

sr-crown-hall.text: Mies van der Rohe finished Crown Hall in 1956 for IIT's architecture school and called it "the clearest structure we have done, the best to express our philosophy." Its roof hangs from four exterior steel girders, so the main floor is a clear span with no interior columns. It was named a National Historic Landmark in 2001.
sr-crown-hall.descriptor: Mies van der Rohe's 1956 glass-and-steel home for IIT architecture

stans-donuts-coffee.text: Stan's is a transplant with two families behind it: Chicago baker Rich Labriola, of Labriola Baking Company, partnered with Stan Berman, who founded the original Stan's Donuts in Los Angeles, and brought the name here in 2014. The Chocolate Lightning is the house signature.
stans-donuts-coffee.descriptor: Donut and coffee shop; LA's Stan's, Chicago-made since 2014

stans-donuts-coffee-chicago-loop.text: Chicago baker Rich Labriola brought Stan's here in 2014 by partnering with Stan Berman, who founded the original Stan's in Los Angeles. The Wicker Park shop is known for filled "pocket" donuts — the Biscoff cookie-butter one especially — plus the buttermilk bar and the Chocolate Lightning.
stans-donuts-coffee-chicago-loop.descriptor: Donut and coffee shop at Damen & North Ave. in Wicker Park

stans-donuts-coffee-streeterville-east-e.text: Stan's is a Chicago–Los Angeles mashup: Rich Labriola of Labriola Baking Company opened the first Chicago shop in 2014 in partnership with Stan Berman, founder of the original Stan's Donuts in Los Angeles. The Chocolate Lightning is the shop's signature.
stans-donuts-coffee-streeterville-east-e.descriptor: Donut and coffee shop on North Clark Street in Lakeview

writtenFor.name: Stan's Donuts & Coffee - Lake View East (North Clark Street)

stans-donuts-coffee-west-town.text: Stan's began as Stan Berman's shop in Los Angeles. In 2014 Rich Labriola of Labriola Baking Company opened the first Chicago Stan's Donuts & Coffee out of that partnership, and the Chocolate Lightning is its signature donut.
stans-donuts-coffee-west-town.descriptor: Donut and coffee shop on E. Erie St. by Northwestern's downtown campus

writtenFor.name: Stan's Donuts & Coffee - Streeterville (East Erie Street)

stax-cafe-little-italy.text: Owner Spiro Tsaldaris runs Stax with his wife Heather and their daughters Penelope and Mila. He grew up in his father's Chicago diner, which stayed open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. The breakfast-focused kitchen — all-day breakfast and breakfast-leaning lunch, with locations in Little Italy and River West — has been Michelin-recommended six years running.
stax-cafe-little-italy.descriptor: Family-run all-day breakfast cafe with Little Italy and River West locations

steppenwolf-ensemble-theatre.text: Jeff Perry, Terry Kinney and Gary Sinise founded Steppenwolf in a Highland Park school basement in 1974; the ensemble now runs to 51 members and has included John Malkovich, Laurie Metcalf, Joan Allen and Tracy Letts. The company holds the National Medal of Arts and 14 Tony Awards, and Letts's "August: Osage County" premiered here before winning Best Play on Broadway.
steppenwolf-ensemble-theatre.descriptor: Ensemble theater on N. Halsted in Lincoln Park, founded 1974

steppenwolf-theatre.text: Steppenwolf started in 1974 in the basement of a Unitarian church in Deerfield, founded by Terry Kinney, Jeff Perry and Gary Sinise, and named for the Hermann Hesse novel one member happened to be reading during the first production. Its ensemble has included John Malkovich, Laurie Metcalf, Joan Allen and Tracy Letts, whose August: Osage County won five Tony Awards.
steppenwolf-theatre.descriptor: Lincoln Park theater company on N. Halsted, founded 1974

strings-ramen.text: Strings makes its noodles fresh every day on a dough mixer and noodle maker imported straight from Japan, and sticks to ramen rather than a broader menu. The Chinatown original at 2141 S Archer Ave, across from New Chinatown Square, also serves oden, the Japanese winter appetizer. First come, first served — no reservations.
strings-ramen.descriptor: Chinatown ramen shop on Archer Ave with noodles made fresh daily

strings-ramen-armour-square.text: Strings makes its noodles fresh every day on a dough mixer and noodle machine imported from Japan. It's a small chain with Chicago shops in Hyde Park, Lincoln Park and Chinatown plus Madison, West Lafayette and Aurora, and it takes no reservations — seating is first come, first served.
strings-ramen-armour-square.descriptor: Ramen shop at 1453 E. 53rd St. in Hyde Park, noodles made in house daily

sultans-market.text: Started in 1995 as a small family shop in Wicker Park by Shadi Ramli and his mother, who emigrated from Jordan in the 1980s. The falafel made its name — a repeat Chicago Reader Best Falafel winner — and the original counter at 2057 W. North Ave. has since grown to locations in Lincoln Park, Logan Square and Pilsen.
sultans-market.descriptor: Middle Eastern falafel counter on North Ave in Wicker Park since 1995

sun-wah-bar-b-que.text: Lynda and Eric Cheng opened Sun Wah in 1986, and their children Kelly, Laura and Michael took it over in 2008. The off-menu Beijing Duck Feast — duck carved tableside, then the carcass returned as fried rice or noodles, then soup — won the restaurant a James Beard America's Classics award in 2018.
sun-wah-bar-b-que.descriptor: Cantonese BBQ in Uptown since 1986, famed for its Beijing duck feast

sunda-new-asian.descriptor: Pan-Asian restaurant and lounge in River North from Rockit Ranch Productions

superdawg.text: Maurie and Flaurie Berman opened this drive-in in 1948 and mounted two giant anthropomorphic hot dogs on the roof, Maurie and Flaurie, named for the founders. Carhops still deliver orders on trays that hook onto the car window, and the Superdawg comes in a box with crinkle-cut fries and a pickled green tomato instead of the usual Chicago tomato slice.
superdawg.descriptor: Carhop drive-in at Milwaukee, Devon and Nagle since 1948

sushi-san-lincoln-park.text: The Lincoln Park outpost of Sushi-san, the Lettuce Entertain You sushi group that started in River North and also runs a counter in Willis Tower. Master sushi chef Kaze Chan oversees the menu, and the room is built around a bar with floor-to-ceiling glass that opens onto a patio on Halsted, plus one of the largest sake-by-the-glass lists in the city.
sushi-san-lincoln-park.descriptor: Lettuce Entertain You sushi bar at 1950 N Halsted in Lincoln Park

sushi-taku-logan-square.descriptor: All-you-can-eat sushi on Milwaukee Ave in Logan Square

sushidokku.text: Sushi Dokku serves elevated Japanese cuisine and "chef dressed" nigiri, including A5 wagyu, at 823 W. Randolph in the West Loop. Downstairs, a hidden bar called Booze Box runs as its own venue with separate evening hours.
sushidokku.descriptor: Modern sushi bar on West Loop's Randolph Row

swift-sons.text: Swift & Sons is named for Gustavus Franklin Swift, the 19th-century pioneer of Chicago's cattle trade, and the building it occupies at 1000 W. Fulton Market was once a cold storage facility in the middle of the city's meatpacking district. It was created by Boka Restaurant Group with B. Hospitality, executive chef Chris Pandel and design firm Avroko, whose interior evokes a turn-of-the-century office building.
swift-sons.descriptor: Boka Group steakhouse at 1000 W. Fulton Market in a former cold-storage house

symphony-center.text: Daniel Burnham designed Orchestra Hall, which opened December 14, 1904 as the home of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra; the facade still reads "Theodore Thomas Orchestra Hall" for the orchestra's first music director. It was made a National Historic Landmark in 1994, and a $110 million expansion completed in 1997 wrapped it into the larger Symphony Center complex. Harry Houdini, Amelia Earhart and Orson Welles all spoke from its stage.
symphony-center.descriptor: Chicago Symphony Orchestra's Michigan Avenue concert hall, open since 1904

taco-burrito-king-west-loop.text: Taco Burrito King started in 1992 as a single small stand and grew into a family-run chain of Chicagoland taquerias serving fresh, home-style Mexican food seven days a week, 365 days a year, with several locations open around the clock. This one sits on Jackson Boulevard in Greektown, at the edge of the West Loop.
taco-burrito-king-west-loop.descriptor: Family-run Mexican counter on W. Jackson Blvd, Chicago chain since 1992

taco-burrito-king-west-touhy-avenue.text: Taco Burrito King started in 1992 with a single location and grew into a Chicagoland chain that operates year-round, with several stores open 24 hours. The company says its main facility was the first restaurant in the country to use solar panels to directly heat its water, alongside permeable parking pavers and energy-efficient equipment.
taco-burrito-king-west-touhy-avenue.descriptor: Chicago-area taqueria chain on W. Touhy Ave; several stores open 24 hours

writtenFor.name: Taco Burrito King - West Touhy Avenue

tamale-lady.descriptor: Mexican tamale cart on S. Blue Island Ave in Pilsen

tango-sur.text: Tango Sur is the Southport Avenue Argentine grill founded by Sergio Di Sapio, whose family also runs Folklore, Ñ, Bodega Sur and El Mercado. Everything centers on the parrilla: authentic wood-fired asado and grilled meats with housemade chimichurri, alongside handmade pastas and empanadas.
tango-sur.descriptor: Argentine parrilla steakhouse on Southport Ave in Lakeview

tanta.text: Tanta is the Chicago restaurant of Peruvian chef Gastón Acurio, whose Lima flagship Astrid y Gastón topped Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants in 2013 and whose group now runs more than 70 venues in 10 countries. The W. Grand room has a second-floor private dining room and a seasonal rooftop terrace.
tanta.descriptor: Peruvian restaurant with a rooftop terrace at 118 W. Grand, River North

taqueria-el-milagro.text: El Milagro has been making tortillas in Chicago since 1950, founded by Raul Lopez, who was orphaned at 11 and learned the trade from his uncle Miguel, a leading corn miller in Mexico City. The company still grinds carefully selected whole-kernel corn in its own plant instead of using pre-processed corn flour.
taqueria-el-milagro.descriptor: Counter taqueria beside the El Milagro tortilla plant on W. 26th St

taqueria-los-comales.text: Los Comales started in 1973 on 26th Street in Little Village and bills itself as one of Chicago's first taquerías. It has since spread into a set of neighborhood taco counters across the city, including this one in Pilsen.
taqueria-los-comales.descriptor: Taco counter on 18th Street in Pilsen; the chain dates to 1973

writtenFor.name: Taqueria Los Comales - Lower West Side

taquieria-atotonilco.text: Brothers Oscar and Raul Muñoz started Atotonilco in 1972 as a small taco stand in Chicago's Little Village, and Oscar later added an on-site tortillería so the tortillas are made fresh in house. The Pilsen shop on Blue Island Avenue serves tacos, tortas and licuados, and caters meat trays and taco platters.
taquieria-atotonilco.descriptor: Family taquería and tortillería on Blue Island Ave in Pilsen

taste-of-peru.text: An unassuming Clark Street strip-mall storefront that opens into a dining room hung with Peruvian art. The kitchen is known for a heaping mixed ceviche of calamari, shrimp, octopus and mussels, along with lomo saltado.
taste-of-peru.descriptor: Peruvian home cooking in a Rogers Park strip mall on Clark St

tavern-on-rush.text: An upscale American steakhouse anchoring the Rush Street strip in the Gold Coast, serving prime steaks and seafood from breakfast until late. Time Out describes the worn brown leather and dark polished wood as "Ivy League kind of pomp" — until a football game turns the room "as dignified as a locker room."
tavern-on-rush.descriptor: Gold Coast steakhouse on Rush Street, open from breakfast to late

thalia-hall.text: Saloonkeeper John Dusek built Thalia Hall in 1892 as a mixed-use block - storefronts, apartments and a grand public hall for Pilsen's Bohemian immigrants - with architects Faber & Pagels modeling the theater on Prague's opera house. It closed in the 1960s and sat dormant until Bruce Finkelman and Craig Golden reopened it in 2013 as a music venue with bars including the basement Punch House.
thalia-hall.descriptor: 1892 Pilsen hall on S Allport St, now a concert venue and bar complex

the-art-institute-of-chicago.text: Founded in 1879, the museum has occupied its Grant Park building since 1893, guarded by Edward Kemeys's two bronze lions unveiled in 1894 (one 'on the prowl,' one 'in an attitude of defiance'). Inside hang Grant Wood's American Gothic, Hopper's Nighthawks, bought nearly new in 1942 for $3,000, and Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.
the-art-institute-of-chicago.descriptor: Encyclopedic art museum on Michigan Ave with the bronze lions, founded 1879

the-art-of-pizza.text: A plain storefront on Ashland that has spent more than 30 years making pan pizza — and, unusually for Chicago deep dish, selling it by the slice. The Chicago Tribune voted its deep dish #1 in the city, praising a "near-perfect, golden-brown crust."
the-art-of-pizza.descriptor: Lakeview deep-dish and stuffed pizza sold by the slice on N. Ashland

the-aviary.text: Grant Achatz's Alinea Group opened The Aviary in 2011 as a bar run like a restaurant kitchen: drinks are built in a fenced-off "cocktail kitchen" rather than behind a bar, with custom glassware and a dedicated ice program. It won the James Beard Award for Outstanding Bar Program in 2013.
the-aviary.descriptor: Alinea Group's high-concept cocktail lab on W Fulton Market since 2011

the-berghoff-restaurant.text: Herman Joseph Berghoff, an immigrant from Dortmund, opened the place in 1898, and it still serves sauerbraten, schnitzel and creamed spinach. When Prohibition ended in 1933 the Berghoff was issued Chicago's Liquor License No. 1. Its men's-only bar held out until 1969, when members of the National Organization for Women, Gloria Steinem among them, walked in and demanded service.
the-berghoff-restaurant.descriptor: German restaurant on W. Adams in the Loop since 1898

the-bongo-room.text: The Bongo Room opened July 5, 1993 in a spot off Damen Avenue before settling at 1470 N. Milwaukee, and built its reputation on seasonally changing pancakes and french toast — the sweet, over-the-top brunch plates that still pull weekend lines. A few day-one items survive on the menu, including the breakfast burrito and the croissant sandwiches.
the-bongo-room.descriptor: Wicker Park brunch spot on Milwaukee Ave known for pancakes, since 1993

the-butterfly-house.text: A mesh-walled garden enclosure on Navy Pier's North Lawn holds live butterflies from around the world — stand still and one may land on you. Its chrysalises come from conservation-minded breeders including El Bosque Nuevo in Costa Rica, which has protected over 1,000 acres of rainforest, and Alas de Colombia, a woman-owned Colombian operation.
the-butterfly-house.descriptor: Walk-through butterfly exhibit on Navy Pier's North Lawn

the-chicago-diner.text: Mickey Hornick and Chef Jo Kaucher opened the Chicago Diner on Halsted in 1983, when skeptics told them a vegetarian restaurant would never work. The menu is diner food rebuilt without meat: the signature Radical Reuben made with house seitan, veggie burgers and home fries, and the vegan milkshakes that helped make its name.
the-chicago-diner.descriptor: Vegetarian diner at 3411 N Halsted in Lakeview, open since 1983

the-dearborn.text: Irish-born sisters Amy and Clodagh Lawless, who grew up in their family's restaurant in Ireland, opened The Dearborn in 2016 on a Loop corner near the theater district. It's an upscale American tavern run on Irish hospitality, known for its steaks, its burger and its fish 'n' chips.
the-dearborn.descriptor: Upscale American tavern at 145 N. Dearborn in the Loop, opened 2016

the-duck-inn.text: Kevin Hickey's gastro-tavern occupies a pre-Prohibition-era building on the border of Chicago's Bridgeport and Pilsen neighborhoods, at 2701 S. Eleanor. Its signature rotisserie duck can be reserved in advance. The restaurant holds a Michelin Guide Bib Gourmand and was a 2024 James Beard Outstanding Restaurant semifinalist.
the-duck-inn.descriptor: Bridgeport gastro-tavern known for its signature rotisserie duck

the-empty-bottle.text: Bruce Finkelman opened the Empty Bottle in 1992 and moved it to Western Avenue in 1993, where the 400-capacity room became Chicago's home base for underground rock and experimental music - early-career shows there include the White Stripes, Yeah Yeah Yeahs, LCD Soundsystem and Neutral Milk Hotel. It also keeps a house cat; Radley lived on site for about sixteen years.
the-empty-bottle.descriptor: Ukrainian Village indie rock club on N Western Ave since 1992

the-fireplace-inn.descriptor: Old Town barbecue rib house on N. Wells St

the-frontier.descriptor: Wild-game gastropub off Milwaukee Ave in West Town, open since 2011

the-gage.text: The Gage sits in the Gage Group — three 1890s Michigan Avenue buildings raised for the millinery trade by Holabird & Roche, with Louis Sullivan designing the ornamental facade next door at 18 S. Michigan. Vintage hat ads still line the staircase, and the kitchen turns out scotch eggs, fish and chips and a venison burger with Millennium Park out the window.
the-gage.descriptor: Gastropub across from Millennium Park at 24 S. Michigan Ave

the-goddess-and-grocer.text: Debbie Sharpe, who hails from Melbourne, opened the first Goddess and Grocer on Damen Avenue in Bucktown because she wanted the kind of Australian-style deli she missed from home — good coffee, freshly prepared foods, salads, sandwiches and baked goods. The shop at 911 W. Randolph in Fulton Market is one of several that followed, along with Gold Coast and an O'Hare store.
the-goddess-and-grocer.descriptor: Australian-style café and deli at 911 W. Randolph in Fulton Market

writtenFor.name: The Goddess and Grocer - Fulton Market District

the-green-door-tavern.text: The building went up in 1872, a year after the Great Chicago Fire, using the wood-frame construction the city banned downtown soon after — it has been visibly leaning for over a century. It opened as a tavern in 1921, ran as a speakeasy through Prohibition, and the downstairs bar, The Drifter, occupies that original speakeasy room.
the-green-door-tavern.descriptor: River North tavern in a leaning 1872 wood-frame building, bar since 1921

the-hideout.text: A balloon-frame house wedged among factories and a city fleet yard at Ada and Wabansia; by the bar's own account bootleggers ran it before it opened legally in 1934. It has since become one of Chicago's essential small music rooms — Jack White, Neko Case and Andrew Bird have all played it — and it throws an annual anniversary block party.
the-hideout.descriptor: Century-old bar in an industrial corridor; punk, indie and alt-country

the-ledge.text: The Ledge is a set of all-glass boxes that opened July 2, 2009, extending about four feet out from the 103rd floor of Willis Tower, 1,353 feet above South Wacker Drive, so you can look straight down at the street between your shoes. The Skydeck is the highest observation deck in the United States. The glass flooring has cracked underfoot twice, in 2014 and 2019.
the-ledge.descriptor: Glass-floored balconies on the Willis Tower Skydeck, 103rd floor

the-light-of-truth-ida-b-wells-national-.text: Unveiled in 2021 at 37th and South Langley in Bronzeville, Richard Hunt's 35-foot, 14,000-pound bronze-and-granite sculpture stands on the former grounds of the Ida B. Wells Homes and is Chicago's first large-scale monument to a Black woman leader. More than 4,300 donors funded it, and it takes its name from Wells' line that "the way to right wrongs is to turn the light of truth upon them."
the-light-of-truth-ida-b-wells-national-.descriptor: 35-ft Richard Hunt bronze honoring Ida B. Wells, in Bronzeville

writtenFor.name: The Light of Truth Ida B. Wells National Monument

the-lodge-tavern.text: The Lodge opened at 21 W. Division in 1957 and bills itself as the oldest standing establishment in the Gold Coast's Division Street entertainment district. What keeps regulars coming hasn't changed much: beer, a jukebox, and an endless supply of complimentary peanuts.
the-lodge-tavern.descriptor: Gold Coast tavern on Division St. since 1957, with free peanuts

the-loyalist.text: The Loyalist is the relaxed garden-level room below Smyth on Ada Street, where chef John Shields' team cooks with the same care as the three-Michelin-starred restaurant upstairs. Its burger has landed on best-burger lists from Condé Nast Traveler, Delish and Modern Luxury.
the-loyalist.descriptor: Garden-level bistro under Smyth in West Loop, famous for its burger

the-map-room.text: A Bucktown beer bar on Hoyne with a deep craft list that doubles as a coffeehouse in the morning and unveils new or limited specialty releases on Tuesdays.
the-map-room.descriptor: Bucktown craft beer bar on Hoyne that's a coffeehouse in the mornings

the-matchbox.text: The Matchbox is famously small — Time Out likens the room to a boxcar — so the patio next door practically doubles the capacity.
