Drinks lean on fresh lemon and lime juice and house-infused vodkas, and the food comes from the Silver Palm, the railroad dining-car restaurant next door.
the-matchbox.descriptor: Tiny cocktail bar on N. Milwaukee Ave in River West

the-office.text: The Office sits behind an unmarked door below The Aviary at 955 W. Fulton Market, part of Grant Achatz's Alinea Group. The 21-seat room takes reservations only and pours classic cocktails, vintage spirits and luxury bites; the Aviary upstairs won the James Beard Award for Outstanding Bar Program in 2013.
the-office.descriptor: Hidden reservations-only cocktail bar beneath The Aviary, Fulton Market

the-old-post-office.text: Graham, Anderson, Probst & White built the main post office in 1921 and expanded it in 1932 to some 2.5 million square feet - with a hole deliberately left in its base so a future expressway could run straight through the building, which Ida B. Wells Drive now does. Mail operations moved out in 1997 and it sat empty for two decades until a roughly $800 million redevelopment reopened it in 2019 with offices, a rooftop park and a riverwalk.
the-old-post-office.descriptor: 1921 riverside mail behemoth on W Van Buren, now offices with a rooftop park

the-peggy-notebaert-nature-museum.text: Home to the Chicago Academy of Sciences, founded in 1857 as the city's first museum devoted to nature — its original collection burned in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. The current Perkins and Will building opened in 1999 beside North Pond, and its best-known draw is the live butterfly house, home to more than 200 species.
the-peggy-notebaert-nature-museum.descriptor: Chicago Academy of Sciences nature museum by North Pond, Lincoln Park

the-publican.text: One Off Hospitality's Publican has been on Fulton Market since 2008 as, in Time Out's phrase, "a shrine to beer, pork and seafood." Diners sit at long communal tables and in booths built to look like pig pens, and the room itself won a James Beard award for outstanding restaurant design in 2009.
the-publican.descriptor: Beer-hall-style pork and seafood restaurant in Fulton Market since 2008

the-purple-pig.text: The Purple Pig opened on North Michigan Avenue in 2009 serving Mediterranean-inspired small plates meant to be shared, drawing on Italy, Spain, Greece and the Levant. Bon Appetit named it one of the best new restaurants in America the following year, and it has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand every year from 2011 through 2025.
the-purple-pig.descriptor: Mediterranean small plates on N Michigan Ave, open since 2009

the-redhead-piano-bar.text: The Redhead has run live piano seven nights a week on Ontario Street since 1993, staying open until 4 a.m. — 5 a.m. on Saturdays. It also keeps a walk-in humidor stocked with more than 150 cigars and a heated, year-round covered smoking patio, and marked its 30th birthday in June 2023 with a public party that ran from 4 p.m. to midnight.
the-redhead-piano-bar.descriptor: River North piano bar on Ontario St, live piano nightly since 1993

the-rookery.text: Burnham and Root completed it in 1888, and Frank Lloyd Wright remade the skylit lobby in his Prairie style between 1905 and 1907. The name came from the temporary city hall that stood on the site: crows and pigeons flocked to it, and the nickname doubled as a jab at the politicians inside. The light court's glass skylight is composed of some 5,000 panes.
the-rookery.descriptor: 1888 Burnham & Root building in the Loop, lobby remodeled by Frank Lloyd Wright

the-rosebud.text: Alex Dana opened the first Rosebud on Taylor Street in Chicago's Little Italy, originally under the name Bocciola della Rose — 'bud of the rose.' It became known for authentic Italian cooking and a celebrity clientele, and in 2017 Taylor Street was given the honorary designation 'Alex Dana Way.'
the-rosebud.descriptor: Little Italy red-sauce Italian on Taylor St

the-second-city.text: Chicago's original improv theater opened at 1842 North Wells Street in 1959 and moved to 1616 N. Wells in 1967. Its stage launched John Belushi, Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Tina Fey, Amy Poehler, Steve Carell and Stephen Colbert, and the company produced the sketch series SCTV.
the-second-city.descriptor: Improv comedy theater on North Wells in Old Town, since 1959

the-vic.text: Robert E. Ricksen and Frank Gazzolo spent three years and $300,000 building the Vic as a five-story vaudeville house, opened in 1912 as the Victoria Theatre and designed by theater architect John Eberson. Walt Klein bought and renovated it in 1983, and it later moonlighted as "Brew & View" - movies and drinks on nights without a concert - while running as a roughly 1,400-capacity music hall.
the-vic.descriptor: 1912 vaudeville house on N Sheffield, now a 1,400-capacity concert venue

the-wiener-circle.text: The stand opened on Clark Street in Lincoln Park in 1983, but its reputation dates to about 1992, when proprietor Larry Gold started the profane back-and-forth with late-night drunks that became the house style. The routine has since put it on This American Life and Comedy Central's Insomniac with Dave Attell; the actual food is char-grilled Vienna Beef dogs on poppy seed buns.
the-wiener-circle.descriptor: Late-night char dog stand on N Clark known for insulting its customers

the-wild-hare-fulton-market-district.text: The Wild Hare & Singing Armadillo Frog Sanctuary was a reggae bar in Wrigleyville on the North Side before resurfacing at 950 W Fulton Market. It still calls itself rooted in reggae tradition, with live entertainment nightly from a resident house band and rotating DJs.
the-wild-hare-fulton-market-district.descriptor: Reggae-rooted live music bar and club on Fulton Market

writtenFor.name: The Wild Hare - Fulton Market District

the-wormhole-coffee.text: The Wormhole sits at 1462 N. Milwaukee Ave. in Wicker Park, sharing its address with Halfwit Coffee Roasters, the affiliated roastery and whole-bean market whose coffee it pours.
the-wormhole-coffee.descriptor: Wicker Park cafe on Milwaukee Ave sharing its space with Halfwit Coffee Roasters

three-dots-and-a-dash.text: Lettuce Entertain You opened Three Dots and a Dash in 2013 behind a discreet alley door off Hubbard Street in River North, and it was selling about 6,000 drinks a week within its first year. The name is the Morse code signal for the letter V - as in victory, a World War II reference.
three-dots-and-a-dash.descriptor: River North tiki bar down an alley off Hubbard St since 2013

topo-gigio-ristorante.text: Topo Gigio is named for the Italian mouse puppet who was a fixture on The Ed Sullivan Show in the 1960s, and it has served Tuscan-leaning Italian on Wells Street since 1988 — the founder brought his family's recipes from Calabria. Anthony Bourdain ate here for Parts Unknown with Bruce Elliott, owner of the nearby Old Town Ale House. The garden patio is first-come, first-served.
topo-gigio-ristorante.descriptor: Old Town Italian on Wells St since 1988, with a first-come garden patio

topolobampo.text: Rick and Deann Bayless opened Topolobampo in 1989, one of Chicago's first fine-dining Mexican restaurants at a time when regional Mexican cooking rarely got the white-tablecloth treatment in America. It holds a Michelin star, won the James Beard Foundation's Outstanding Restaurant award in 2017, and Bayless was guest chef for the 2010 White House state dinner honoring Mexico's president.
topolobampo.descriptor: Rick Bayless's fine-dining Mexican room on N. Clark St, open since 1989

tortello.text: Dario Monni and Jill Gray's West Division Street spot is three things at once: a counter-service restaurant, a pastificio selling fresh pasta by the pound daily, and an alimentari modeled on Dario's grandfather Alifer's 1960s Venetian specialty shop. It's walk-ins only, and has been featured in the Michelin Guide, on FX's The Bear and on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives.
tortello.descriptor: Handmade pasta counter, pastificio and Italian shop on W. Division St

triple-crown-restaurant.text: Triple Crown has been serving all-day dim sum at 2217 S. Wentworth since 1993, one of Chinatown's standbys for Hong Kong-style cooking, with the kitchen running late on Friday and Saturday nights.
triple-crown-restaurant.descriptor: Chinatown dim sum and Hong Kong cuisine on S Wentworth Ave since 1993

tufanos-vernon-park-tap.text: Open on Vernon Park Place since 1930, Tufano's is one of the last old-school neighborhood Italian taverns left from Chicago's Little Italy, now run by owner Joey DiBuono. The James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2008, and it later turned up on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives.
tufanos-vernon-park-tap.descriptor: Little Italy Italian restaurant on Vernon Park Place since 1930

tuscany.text: Tuscany has anchored Taylor Street for more than a quarter century as part of Phil Stefani Signature Restaurants, cooking Tuscan/Northern Italian around a wood-burning pizza oven and a wood-fired rotisserie. The block is what survives of Chicago's Little Italy, where 200 businesses and 800 homes were bulldozed in the 1960s to build the University of Illinois campus.
tuscany.descriptor: Northern Italian on Taylor Street in Little Italy, wood-fired oven

twin-anchors-restaurant-tavern.text: Twin Anchors has been serving slow-cooked ribs from this Sedgwick Street corner in Old Town since 1932. The restaurant says Frank Sinatra was enough of a regular to get a phone brought to his booth, and the barroom has turned up on screen too, including in Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight and Bonnie Hunt's Return to Me.
twin-anchors-restaurant-tavern.descriptor: Old Town rib joint and tavern on N. Sedgwick, a Chicago institution since 1932

u-505-submarine.text: A US Navy task group boarded and captured U-505 off West Africa on June 4, 1944 — the first enemy warship taken at sea by the Navy since 1815. The haul of charts and codebooks was so sensitive that the whole capture was classified, lest Germany tighten Enigma security on the eve of D-Day. The Navy meant to sink her as target practice; the officer who took her got her donated to the museum instead, dedicated in 1954.
u-505-submarine.descriptor: Captured WWII German U-boat at the Museum of Science and Industry

uncle-remus.text: Founded in 1963, Uncle Remus is one of the West Side counters credited with popularizing Chicago mild sauce — the barbecue-ketchup-hot-sauce blend ladled over fried chicken. In 2019 the Chicago Tribune counted it among the city's iconic Black-owned restaurants, alongside Harold's Chicken Shack and Lem's Bar-B-Q.
uncle-remus.descriptor: West Side saucy fried chicken counter since 1963

uncommon-ground.text: Part coffeehouse, part bar, part restaurant and performance space, Uncommon Ground's Clark Street room in Lakeview is home to Greenstar, billed as the first certified organic brewery in the state, and runs a roughly 70-percent vegetarian menu alongside live music.
uncommon-ground.descriptor: Café, bar and music room at 3800 N Clark in Lakeview

union-stock-yards-gate.text: This limestone arch was the main entrance to the Union Stock Yards, the meatpacking district that made Chicago the center of American meat. Built in 1879 to designs by Daniel Burnham and John Root, it is the only significant structure of the yards to survive their 1971 closing; the plaza beside it honors the 21 firefighters killed in the 1910 stockyard fire. The steer head over the center arch is said to be Sherman, a bull belonging to stockyards superintendent John Sherman.
union-stock-yards-gate.descriptor: 1879 limestone gate on Exchange Ave, last relic of the Union Stock Yards

united-center.text: Opened in 1994 at a cost of $175 million to replace the old Chicago Stadium, it is home to both the Bulls and the Blackhawks and is the largest arena by capacity in the NBA. The Michael Jordan statue 'The Spirit' was dedicated the year it opened and now stands inside a 2017 atrium addition. The arena hosted the Democratic National Convention in 1996 and again in 2024.
united-center.descriptor: Bulls and Blackhawks arena on the Near West Side since 1994

valois.text: Started in 1921 by French Canadian William Valois, this cafeteria-line diner carries the motto "See Your Food" — you point down the steam table and watch your plate get built. It calls itself one of the oldest cafeteria-style restaurants in the country, and it is a well-known Barack Obama haunt.
valois.descriptor: Hyde Park cafeteria-line diner on E 53rd St, founded 1921

victory-monument.text: Erected in 1927, it honors the Eighth Regiment of the Illinois National Guard — the African American unit that fought in France as the 370th U.S. Infantry and was the last regiment pursuing retreating German forces before the 1918 Armistice. A bronze doughboy was added atop the shaft in 1936, and 137 of the regiment's dead are named on a bronze panel.
victory-monument.descriptor: 1927 Bronzeville memorial at 35th & King Drive to Black WWI soldiers

vienna-beef-factory-store.text: Vienna Beef goes back to 1893, when Emil Reichel and Sam Ladany sold hot dogs to crowds at Chicago's World's Columbian Exposition; their frank became the standard for the Chicago-style hot dog. The company moved production out of Bucktown to this Bridgeport plant in 2015, and its factory store sits at the plant on S. Morgan.
vienna-beef-factory-store.descriptor: Vienna Beef's factory store at its Bridgeport plant, 3839 S Morgan St

volare-ristorante-italiano.text: Benny Siddu — who worked in hospitality in Sardinia, mainland Italy, England and on cruise ships before settling in Chicago in 1984 — opened Volare on Grand Avenue in 1997. The name is Italian for "to fly." The kitchen stays traditional with Sardinian touches, and the room seats around 200.
volare-ristorante-italiano.descriptor: Streeterville Italian on Grand Ave since 1997, Sardinian accents

walt-disney-birthplace-house.text: Elias Disney built this house on Tripp Avenue in 1892 for about $800, working from a design his wife Flora drew, and Walt was born in an upstairs bedroom on December 5, 1901. The family moved to Missouri in 1906. A city landmark bid failed in 1991 when the owner of the day fought it and won; later owners restored the house toward its 1901 appearance and opened it for public tours during Open House Chicago in October 2023.
walt-disney-birthplace-house.descriptor: Hermosa house where Walt Disney was born in 1901, now a museum

washington-george-park.text: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux laid out this 372-acre park in the 1870s as the western half of Chicago's South Park scheme, and H.W.S. Cleveland executed the plans after the 1871 fire destroyed the blueprints and drained the budget. Lorado Taft's Fountain of Time — 100 concrete figures streaming past Father Time, dedicated in 1922 — stands at the park's Midway Plaisance edge, and the DuSable Museum occupies the old park administration building.
washington-george-park.descriptor: 372-acre Olmsted-designed South Side park with the Fountain of Time

welles-park.text: Created in 1910 by the Lincoln Park Commission and named for Gideon Welles, Abraham Lincoln's Secretary of the Navy. Its European-style gazebo, wired for lights and sound, is the neighborhood's concert and storytelling stage, and in the 1920s a young Abe Saperstein began coaching basketball at the Welles Park fieldhouse before founding the Harlem Globetrotters.
welles-park.descriptor: Lincoln Square park with a European-style concert gazebo, opened 1910

wendella-tours-dock-3.text: Wendella has been running boats from the river below the Wrigley Building since 1935, when Swedish immigrant Albert Borgstrom bought a fire-damaged hull and rebuilt it into a 97-passenger cruiser. He named it Wendela; the old sailors' superstition against renaming a boat kept the single-L spelling. Still family-run, the company runs its architecture cruises from the dock at 400 N. Michigan Ave.
wendella-tours-dock-3.descriptor: Wendella boat dock at the Wrigley Building, 400 N Michigan Ave

wendella-tours-dock-4.text: The berths under the Wrigley Building have been Wendella's home since 1935, when Swedish immigrant Albert Borgstrom — then working at a Chris-Craft boat shop on Navy Pier — bought a fire-damaged boat and rebuilt it as a 97-passenger cruiser. The family still runs the company, and its 45- and 90-minute Chicago River architecture cruises push off from these docks.
wendella-tours-dock-4.descriptor: Wendella's second riverwalk berth below Michigan Ave at the Wrigley Building

wendella-tours-michigan-avenue.text: Wendella has been running boats from the dock at 400 N. Michigan Avenue — at the Michigan Avenue Bridge beside the Wrigley Building — since 1935, and it's still family-owned. The name began as "Wendela"; a second L was added in the 1950s to make people pronounce it right.
wendella-tours-michigan-avenue.descriptor: Chicago River boat tours from the Wrigley Building dock since 1935

west-argyle-street-historic-district.text: These Uptown blocks were pitched in the 1960s as a "New Chinatown" by restaurateur Jimmy Wong, who planned a mall with pagodas, trees and reflecting ponds. After 1979, organizer Charlie Soo — the unofficial "Mayor of Argyle Street" — remade the strip into a pan-Asian district of Vietnamese, Lao, Cambodian and Chinese businesses. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.
west-argyle-street-historic-district.descriptor: Uptown historic district of Vietnamese, Lao, Cambodian and Chinese businesses

whirlyball.text: WhirlyBall is an actual sport, invented in Utah in the 1960s by Stan Mangum: five-a-side teams drive little electric "Whirlybugs" and use hand scoops to fling a Wiffle ball at a target. Only a handful of North American cities have courts. This Bucktown venue pairs them with bowling, laser tag and a bar with 30-plus craft taps.
whirlyball.descriptor: Bumper-car sport, bowling and laser tag on W Webster Ave in Bucktown

white-palace-grill.text: Open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year since 1939, the White Palace has had only three owners — Arthur Bookman ran it for more than 50 years before selling to George Liakopoulos around 2000. It's one of the last survivors of the old Maxwell Street market area, still fitted with formica booths and gumball machines, and it has turned up on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives and in films including Backdraft.
white-palace-grill.descriptor: 24-hour diner at 1159 S Canal St in the South Loop, open since 1939

wicker-park.text: Brothers Charles G. and Joel H. Wicker set aside this four-acre triangle for the city in 1870, and the neighborhood took the park's name. The grounds first held a small reservoir, then a cut-granite fountain, replaced in 1908 by a wading pool and new trees. By the end of the 19th century the blocks around it were the core of Polish Downtown, nicknamed the Polish Gold Coast.
wicker-park.descriptor: Four-acre triangular park donated in 1870 that gave the neighborhood its name

wildberry.text: Wildberry started in 2004 and grew into a five-restaurant Chicago-area breakfast group built on an outsized pancake and French-toast menu — banana-coconut-cream-pie pancakes, Berry Bliss — plus omelets, benedicts and lunch salads. The same owners run Westwood Tavern and The Evie.
wildberry.descriptor: Pancake and breakfast cafe at 196 E. Pearson in Streeterville, going since 2004

wildberry-pancakes-and-cafe.text: Founded in 2004, Wildberry made its name on specialty pancakes and French toast — banana-coconut-cream-pie pancakes and Berry Bliss stacks — alongside omelets, benedicts and lunch salads. The Loop branch sits in Prudential Plaza at 130 E. Randolph.
wildberry-pancakes-and-cafe.descriptor: Breakfast and brunch cafe in Prudential Plaza at 130 E. Randolph in the Loop

wildfire.text: This River North dining room is the Chicago flagship of Wildfire, the 1940s supper-club concept from Lettuce Entertain You — the group Rich Melman and Jerry Orzoff started in 1971 with R.J. Grunts. The cooking is built on fire: prime rib slow-roasted six hours, cedar-planked salmon in a brown sugar-soy glaze, steaks aged 28 to 35 days.
wildfire.descriptor: 1940s-style supper club for steaks and chops at 159 W Erie, River North

willie-dixon.text: Willie Dixon (1915-1992) was Chess Records' staff songwriter, bassist, producer and talent scout, and wrote or co-wrote more than 500 songs — "Hoochie Coochie Man," "Little Red Rooster," "Spoonful," "I Just Want to Make Love to You" — that Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf made famous and the Rolling Stones carried worldwide. His marker is one of the Bronzeville Walk of Fame plaques set along King Drive between 25th and 35th.
willie-dixon.descriptor: Bronzeville Walk of Fame plaque on King Drive for the Chess Records songwriter

willie-dixons-blues-heaven-foundation.text: Chess Records worked out of this building from 1957 to 1967, and the Rolling Stones named an instrumental after the address — "2120 South Michigan Avenue" — after recording here on their first U.S. tour in 1964. Willie Dixon was Chess's staff songwriter, behind "Hoochie Coochie Man" and "Little Red Rooster"; his widow Marie bought the building in 1993 and opened it as a museum in 1997.
willie-dixons-blues-heaven-foundation.descriptor: Blues museum in the old Chess Records studio at 2120 S Michigan

wintrust-arena.text: Opened in October 2017 across Cermak Road from McCormick Place, the $173 million arena seats about 10,400 and doubles as an events center for the convention campus. DePaul's men's and women's basketball teams play here, and the WNBA's Chicago Sky moved in from suburban Allstate Arena in 2018.
wintrust-arena.descriptor: 10,000-seat arena by McCormick Place; home to DePaul hoops and the Chicago Sky

wishbone.text: Chef Joel Nickson opened Wishbone in July 1990 at 1800 W. Grand with 23 seats and nine stools, hung with paintings by his mother; the 1992 move to 1001 W. Washington helped turn the West Loop into a restaurant district. It served "southern reconstruction cooking" — blackened catfish, Carolina crab cakes, mix-and-match sides — and closed on August 28, 2026 after 36 years.
wishbone.descriptor: Southern "reconstruction cooking" room at 161 N. Jefferson; closed Aug. 2026

wolfys.text: A walk-up North Side stand slinging Chicago-style Vienna Beef dogs, Italian beef and gyros on Peterson Avenue since 1967, and a stop for Andrew Zimmern's Bizarre Foods.
wolfys.descriptor: Vienna Beef hot dog stand on W Peterson Ave since 1967

woodlawn-tap.text: Opened in 1948 by Jimmy Wilson and still called "Jimmy's," this cash-only tavern has served as the University of Chicago's unofficial common room — the guest book logs Dylan Thomas on March 16, 1950, plus Saul Bellow, Mike Royko and the Compass Players. Wilson refused to stock Budweiser after a pricing dispute with the distributor, and the bar never has since.
woodlawn-tap.descriptor: Cash-only Hyde Park dive known as Jimmy's, on E 55th St since 1948

wrigley-field.text: Opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park for a Federal League club, it is the second-oldest ballpark in the majors after Fenway and the oldest in the National League. The Boston ivy on the outfield brick and the center-field scoreboard both date to 1937, and that scoreboard is still worked by hand from inside.
wrigley-field.descriptor: Cubs ballpark in Wrigleyville since 1914, ivy walls and hand-turned scoreboard

wrigley-field-marquee.text: The marquee went up over Wrigley's main entrance in 1934, and it wasn't always red: the original was green, repainted to the familiar red on March 23, 1960. The ballpark itself opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park. The sign was temporarily removed and restored for the 2016 season, and the CTA paints its image on the wall at the Addison platform to mark the stop.
wrigley-field-marquee.descriptor: Red art deco sign over Wrigley Field's entrance at Clark and Addison

wrigley-rooftops.text: Fans have watched Cubs games from these Waveland and Sheffield rooftops since the 1929 World Series, with the first paying customers in 1938. Owners turned them into real businesses by the mid-1980s, adding bleacher seating; the Cubs pushed back in 2003 with a view-blocking screen nicknamed the "spite fence" and a lawsuit, settled in 2004 when the rooftops agreed to pay the team 17% of gross revenue.
wrigley-rooftops.descriptor: Rooftop bleachers overlooking Wrigley Field from Sheffield and Waveland

xoco.text: Xoco — pronounced "SHO-ko," the Aztec word for "little sister" — is the fast, casual counterpart to Rick and Deann Bayless's Frontera Grill and Topolobampo in River North. It opens early and closes late on Mexican street food: crusty tortas, meal-in-a-bowl caldos, flaky empanadas, hot-from-the-fryer churros and frothy Mexican hot chocolate.
xoco.descriptor: Rick Bayless's Mexican street-food café in River North

xurro-lower-west-side.text: Xurro has been frying churros to order since 1996, made from scratch with no lard, no artificial flavors and no premade mixes: classic cinnamon-sugar sticks, ones filled with Bavarian cream or Nutella, and churro sundaes. From a Chicago start it has grown to about 13 shops across four states.
xurro-lower-west-side.descriptor: Made-to-order churro shop at 2214 S. Wolcott in Pilsen, going since 1996

yolk.text: Yolk started in Chicago's South Loop in 2006, when Taki Kastanis — who opened his first breakfast-and-lunch spot at 20, then detoured through real estate — bet on an upscale breakfast-and-lunch room downtown. It caught on fast, taking Citysearch's "Best Breakfast" honors in 2008, and grew into locations across Chicago, Texas and Florida.
yolk.descriptor: Breakfast and lunch at 1120 S Michigan Ave — the first Yolk, opened 2006

yolk-west-loop.text: Taki Kastanis, who grew up in his parents' restaurants, opened the first Yolk in the South Loop in 2006; within two years it was taking "best breakfast" honors from Citysearch and Fox Chicago viewers, and the brand spread to other cities. The West Loop store is one of four Yolks in Chicago.
yolk-west-loop.descriptor: All-day breakfast and brunch cafe at 500 W. Madison; Chicago chain since 2006

zebra-lounge.text: A single room hidden on the ground floor of the Canterbury Court apartment building on State Street, between Division and Scott in the Gold Coast. A pianist plays standards nightly under deep red lighting, and Time Out has described the crowd as singles, socialites and sexagenarians.
zebra-lounge.descriptor: One-room piano bar inside a Gold Coast apartment building on N State St

stellas-diner.text: A Lakeview diner on N Broadway that served the neighborhood for decades under Marvin Barsky, who also owns The Bagel deli across the street. It closed temporarily in mid-2026 after a failed city health inspection, then closed permanently when Barsky sold it to Ann Sather owner Tom Tunney — Lakeview's 44th Ward alderperson for two decades — who plans to renovate and reopen the space as an Ann Sather.
stellas-diner.descriptor: Longtime Lakeview diner on N Broadway; closed in 2026, becoming an Ann Sather
